fields.title: Portraits of Courage – Elisabeth Elliot
fields.subtitle: A Widow in the Forest, a Writer Who Would Not Pretend, and a Long Obedience
fields.description: A Christian biography of Elisabeth Elliot (1926–2015), the missionary linguist whose husband Jim was killed by the Waorani of Ecuador in 1956, and who two years later carried their small daughter into the forest to live among the men who had done it. It follows her through Shandia and the Waorani clearings, her honest books and questions, two more marriages and a second widowhood, Gateway to Joy, and her last years. An independent Ochorus life, not endorsed by her estate; all Scripture from the public-domain King James Version.
fields.about_html:
This is a biography of Elisabeth Elliot, not a book by her. Written by Ochorus as the eighth volume of Portraits of Courage, it tells her whole life in narrative: the Brussels birth and the Philadelphia home ordered by Scripture and hymns; a Florida boarding school and Greek at Wheaton; a five-year courtship with Jim Elliot laid, by both of them, on the altar; a first year in Ecuador among the Colorado people that ended in a murder and a stolen suitcase; marriage and the Quichua work at Shandia; the deaths of Jim and four friends on the Curaray in January 1956; the two Waorani women who came to live in her house, and the October day in 1958 when she carried her small daughter into the forest to live among the people who had killed her husband; her return to America, her honest novel and her questions; two more marriages and a second widowhood; Gateway to Joy, the newsletter and the books; and the long twilight of dementia that ended at Magnolia on 15 June 2015.

It is an independent work. It is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by Elisabeth Elliot’s family, her estate, or any company that holds rights in her writings. Her books are still in copyright and should be obtained from their publishers. This book tells her life in its own words and does not quote her writings; the only words of the Elliots it quotes are one well-known sentence from Jim Elliot’s journal. Her teaching is set out in a separate Ochorus companion, The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot.

Where the sources disagree, on what happened on the sandbar on 8 January 1956, on the years among the Waorani and her parting from Rachel Saint, or on the hard years of her third marriage, the book says so and gives the main accounts fairly. It is written with gratitude but not hagiography: she was brave, candid and disciplined, and she could also be stern, guarded and hard to know. All Scripture is from the King James Version. It ends with lessons from her life, a study guide, a chronology, and a note on sources with further reading, including the public-domain writers she loved that are in the Ochorus library: Amy Carmichael and David Brainerd among them.

qa.question: What is this biography of Elisabeth Elliot about?
qa.answer: It is a Christian biography of Elisabeth Elliot (1926–2015), the missionary and writer whose husband Jim was killed with four other men by the Waorani of Ecuador in January 1956. It follows her whole life: her childhood in a Bible-centred home, Wheaton and the long courtship, her first missionary work, Shandia, the deaths on the Curaray, her years living among the Waorani, her return to America, her books and broadcasts, her second and third marriages, and her death in 2015.

qa.question: Who was Elisabeth Elliot?
qa.answer: Elisabeth Howard was born in Brussels in 1926 to American missionary parents and grew up near Philadelphia. She studied Greek at Wheaton College to become a Bible translator, went to Ecuador in 1952, and married Jim Elliot there in 1953. After his death she lived among the Waorani, then returned to the United States in 1963 and became one of the most widely read Christian writers and speakers of her generation, through books such as Through Gates of Splendor and Passion and Purity and the radio programme Gateway to Joy.

qa.question: Is this book connected with Elisabeth Elliot’s family or estate?
qa.answer: No. It is an independent biography, not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by her family, her estate, or any company that holds rights in her writings. Her books are still in copyright and should be obtained from their publishers. This book tells her life in its own words and does not quote her writings.

qa.question: How does this book differ from The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot?
qa.answer: The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot sets out what she taught: the sovereignty and love of God, doing the next thing, suffering offered back to God, obedience, discipline, purity, loneliness and the quiet heart. This book is a narrative life. It tells what happened to her and to the people around her, and touches her teaching only where it is part of the story.

qa.question: Why did Elisabeth Elliot go to live among the Waorani?
qa.answer: She had gone to Ecuador to give an unwritten people the Scriptures, and after Jim’s death she believed the work he had died attempting was still God’s work. In 1957 two Waorani women came out of the forest and lived in her home, where she learned their language. In October 1958 she went with them, with her three-year-old daughter Valerie and with Rachel Saint, to live among the Waorani, including men who had taken part in the killings.

qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a passage from the King James Version that carries its theme, and further passages are woven through the story. The appendices include lessons from her life, each resting on Scripture, a chapter-by-chapter study guide and a chronology.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
“When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.”

— Isaiah 43:2, KJV

The earlier volumes of this series told of a Chinese church leader who died in a Communist labour camp, an American who prayed his way through the villages of the Punjab, a Dutch watchmaker who hid Jews behind a false wall, a Scottish mill girl who went alone up the rivers of Calabar, an African bishop who had once been sold as a slave, an Indian widow who built a home for thousands of outcast women, and an Oxford don who was found by God against his will. This eighth volume tells the story of a woman whose name, for most of the people who know it at all, is attached to a single week in January 1956, when her husband and four other young missionaries were killed on a sandbar in the Ecuadorian rainforest.

Elisabeth Elliot was twenty-nine that week, with a daughter of ten months. She lived for almost sixty years more. This book is about the whole of that life, before the sandbar and after it, and it is written in the conviction that the courage of the long years was no smaller than the courage of the short one.

Why Courage?

Some of her courage was of the kind the world recognises. Less than three years after the killings, she walked into the forest with her three-year-old daughter to live among the very people whose men had speared her husband, sleeping in their houses, eating their food and learning their unwritten language. Many people admired the decision, and a good many thought it reckless. She made it anyway, quietly, and she lived with its consequences.

But there was another kind of courage in her that is easier to overlook, and it may have cost her more. It was the courage of candour. Elisabeth Elliot would not let the story of 1956 be told more neatly than it had happened. She wrote a novel about a missionary whose best efforts end in a death she has caused, and it disturbed many of the readers who had loved her first book. She admitted in print that she did not understand why God had allowed what he allowed, and she refused to supply the tidy explanations that others found comforting. Late in life she added a frank epilogue to the most famous book she ever wrote, acknowledging that the sequel among the Waorani had been far more tangled than the first telling suggested. For a woman whose public standing rested on that story, this was not a small thing.

There was courage, too, in simply going on. She was widowed twice: Jim Elliot was killed after twenty-seven months of marriage, and her second husband, Addison Leitch, died of cancer after less than five years. She married a third time, and she kept writing, speaking and broadcasting for decades, often to people whose suffering she knew from the inside. And at the end she went through the slow loss of her own mind, in the care of a husband who stayed beside her. The long obedience of a life is not dramatic. It is made of ordinary days and next things. But it is not easy, and it is not small.

What This Book Is

This book is a narrative life. It follows Elisabeth Howard from her birth in Brussels in 1926 to her death in Magnolia, Massachusetts, in 2015, and it tries to give the people around her their due: her parents, her four brothers and her sister, the headmistress who took a shy girl in hand, Jim Elliot and his companions, the Colorado and Quichua people among whom she first worked, the Waorani women who led her into the forest, Rachel Saint, Valerie, and the two men she married after Jim. It is not an account of her teaching. A companion volume in the Ochorus library, The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot, sets out what she believed and taught about suffering, obedience, discipline, singleness, marriage and the sovereignty of God. The present book touches her ideas only where they are part of the story of her life.

A Word About Her Words

That is not only a matter of arrangement. Elisabeth Elliot’s books, letters, newsletters and broadcasts are still in copyright, and those who hold the rights in them are entitled to guard them. This book is an independent Ochorus biography. It is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by her family, her estate, or any publisher or organisation that holds rights in her writings. It tells her life in its own words. It quotes her only in a handful of very short sentences, each given with its source, and where it reports what she thought or felt it does so in paraphrase. Her books are named so that readers can find them, and readers are warmly encouraged to buy them, or borrow them from a library, and hear her for themselves. Her prose was spare, exact and often surprising, and no summary can stand in for it.

How This Book Is Written

Elisabeth Elliot told parts of her own story many times, and she was an unusually honest witness. But she was also a writer who shaped her material, and in recent years her own journals and letters, now opened to her authorised biographer and edited in part by her daughter, have filled in a fuller and sometimes different picture. Historians of the Waorani mission have added their own careful accounts. Where the sources agree, this book follows them. Where they differ, it says so and gives the main views fairly. It does not invent dialogue, and it does not put thoughts into anyone’s head that the sources do not support.

Gratitude runs through these pages, but this is not a book of praise. Elisabeth Elliot could be brusque, and some who worked with her found her hard. Her views on women and marriage were, and are, contested by Christians who love Scripture as much as she did. She made decisions that others would have made differently, and she would have been the first to say that she was a sinner saved by grace. A portrait that left out the shadows would not be a portrait of her, and it would not have pleased her.

Scripture in This Book

As in the earlier volumes of this series, all Scripture is quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version, the Bible of the household in which she grew up, which is in the public domain. Each chapter opens with a passage that carries its theme.

The verse at the head of this preface is a promise she knew well. It does not say that God’s people will be kept out of the waters or the fire. It says that they will pass through them, and that he will be with them there. Elisabeth Elliot’s life was a long passing through, and this book is the story of how she found that promise to be true.

fields.title: Introduction: The Story Everyone Knows, and the Woman Who Kept Correcting It
fields.body_html:
“And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”

— John 8:32, KJV

The Story Everyone Knows

In January 1956 five young American missionaries were killed by Waorani warriors on a sandbar of the Curaray River in the rainforest of eastern Ecuador. Their names were Jim Elliot, Pete Fleming, Ed McCully, Roger Youderian and Nate Saint. They had spent months preparing to make friendly contact with a people who were feared by their neighbours for killing outsiders, and who had been known to the outside world by a Quichua word, “Auca”, meaning something like savage. The men called their plan Operation Auca. The people themselves use the name Waorani, which this book uses throughout. For several days the contact seemed to be going well. Then, on Sunday 8 January, the men were speared to death.

The story went round the world. Life magazine ran a long photo essay with pictures by Cornell Capa. Newspapers and radio stations carried it. Christian magazines and pulpits across America told and retold it, and within a few years the deaths had become, for a whole generation of evangelicals, the defining missionary story of the century. Thousands of young people dedicated their lives to missionary service because of it. The five men became heroes, and their widows became symbols of faithful grief.

At the centre of the telling stood one of the widows, Elisabeth Elliot. It was she who wrote the book, Through Gates of Splendor, published in 1957, which fixed the story in the minds of millions. It was she who edited her husband’s journals and wrote his life in Shadow of the Almighty the following year. And it was she who, with her small daughter and Nate Saint’s sister Rachel, went to live among the Waorani in 1958. To many readers the sequel seemed to complete the story perfectly: the killers were converted, the widow forgave, the gospel came to the forest, and the sacrifice was vindicated.

The Woman Who Kept Correcting It

The remarkable thing is that the woman who did more than anyone to tell that story spent much of the rest of her life gently, and sometimes not so gently, declining to let it be simplified. She did not deny that God had worked. She believed to the end that he had. But she would not pretend that she could trace all his purposes, and she grew uneasy with versions of the story in which every death had a visible payoff and every loose end was tied.

Her time among the Waorani taught her that people do not divide neatly into the converted and the unconverted, that missionaries carry their own culture and their own sins into the forest with them, and that relations between fellow workers can be as hard as anything in the jungle. Her novel No Graven Image, published in 1966, told of a missionary linguist whose good intentions end in disaster, and many readers who had loved Through Gates of Splendor were dismayed. She wrote of her early losses in These Strange Ashes without pretending to understand them. And when Through Gates of Splendor was reissued in 1996, she added an epilogue that acknowledged, plainly, that events among the Waorani had not unfolded in the simple way that admirers liked to imagine.

That candour is one of the reasons for this book. It would be easy to write a life of Elisabeth Elliot that was really a tribute to a legend. It would also be untrue to her. She spent decades telling Christians that God is to be trusted precisely because he is God, not because he explains himself, and that faith which depends on happy endings is not yet faith. A biography that smoothed away the hard places in her own story would contradict the very thing she spent her life saying.

The Sources

There are, broadly, four kinds of source for her life. The first is her own books. Besides those already named, the most important for the story told here are The Savage My Kinsman (1961), her photographic account of life among the Waorani; These Strange Ashes (1975), about her first year in Ecuador; Passion and Purity (1984), about her long courtship with Jim; The Shaping of a Christian Family (1992), about the home in which she grew up; and many shorter pieces in her newsletter and elsewhere. These are invaluable, but they were written for particular purposes, often many years after the events, by a writer who chose carefully what to tell.

The second is Jim Elliot’s own journals and letters. She drew on them for Shadow of the Almighty and later edited a fuller selection as The Journals of Jim Elliot (1978). In 2019 their daughter, Valerie Elliot Shepard, published a large selection of her parents’ letters to each other in Devotedly, which lets readers see the courtship and early marriage in their own words.

The third, and the most important development since her death, is the authorised biography by Ellen Vaughn, written with full access to Elisabeth Elliot’s private journals and letters: Becoming Elisabeth Elliot (2020), which takes the story to the end of her years in Ecuador, and Being Elisabeth Elliot (2023), which covers the rest of her life. Vaughn’s volumes add a great deal that Elisabeth Elliot never published, including her private struggles, her doubts and her difficult relationships, and this book is indebted to them throughout.

The fourth is the work of others who were there or who have studied the events closely: the widows’ own memories, Russell Hitt’s life of Nate Saint, Olive Fleming Liefeld’s account of the years before and after 1956, and the historian Kathryn Long’s careful study of the Waorani mission, God in the Rainforest (2019). These do not always agree with one another, or with Elisabeth Elliot’s own account.

How This Book Handles Disagreement

Where these sources differ on a date, a name or the order of events, this book either follows the weight of the evidence and says so, or simply notes that accounts differ. Where they differ in judgement, as they do about Rachel Saint, about the methods of the Waorani mission, and about Elisabeth Elliot’s own decisions, it tries to set out the main views fairly without pretending to settle what cannot be settled. It does not invent conversations or scenes, and it does not claim to know what anyone was thinking unless they said so.

It also tries to remember that the story does not belong only to the missionaries. The Waorani had their own history, their own fears and their own reasons for what they did, and in later years some of them told their side of events to those who would listen. Their accounts, gathered by missionaries and historians, have changed the way the story of 1956 is understood. Where they bear on Elisabeth Elliot’s life, this book takes them into account.

The verse at the head of this introduction is the word of Jesus to those who believed on him. It was a word she took seriously. She believed that the truth, including the truth about one’s own story, is not a threat to faith but its friend. The pages that follow try to tell her story in that spirit.

fields.title: Brussels and Germantown
fields.body_html:
“The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.”

— Psalm 16:6, KJV

Born Abroad

Elisabeth Howard was born on 21 December 1926 in Brussels, the capital of Belgium. She was not Belgian. Her parents, Philip Eugene Howard Jr. and Katharine Gillingham Howard, were Americans from the Philadelphia area who had gone to Belgium as missionaries soon after their marriage in 1922, and who worked for some five years with the Belgian Gospel Mission, an evangelical mission founded during the First World War. Belgium was a Roman Catholic country still recovering from the German occupation and the devastation of the western front, and the small Protestant missions there were a very small presence in it.

She was the second of their children. A brother, Philip, had been born before her. Within a few months of her birth, when she was still a baby, her parents left Belgium and returned to the United States. She therefore had no memory of the country where she was born, and she grew up wholly American. But she was born, as it were, on the mission field, to parents who had already given some years of their lives to it, and she would later come to see that fact as more than an accident of geography.

To her family and friends she was Betty, and Betty she remained to them for most of her life. The world later came to know her as Elisabeth Elliot, and it is by that name that this book will mostly call her. But it is worth remembering that the shy, tall, serious girl of the chapters that follow was Betty Howard, and that many of the letters she wrote and received before her marriage were addressed to that name.

A Family and a Paper

What took the family home was a family enterprise of an unusual kind. For half a century the Howard family and their relatives had been bound up with the Sunday School Times, a weekly paper published in Philadelphia that provided Bible lessons, articles and comment for Sunday school teachers in churches of many denominations across America. At its height it was one of the most widely read evangelical papers in the country.

fields.title: A House Ordered by Scripture
fields.body_html:
“And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.”

— Deuteronomy 6:6-7, KJV

A Book About a Home

More than sixty years after she left it, Elisabeth Elliot wrote a book about the home in which she grew up. The Shaping of a Christian Family was published in 1992, a few years after her mother’s death, when she herself was a grandmother many times over. It is not a memoir in the ordinary sense. It is a portrait of a household, drawn from her own memories, from those of her brothers and sister, and from family letters and papers, and it was written with a purpose: to show younger Christian parents what one ordinary home, ordered by Scripture, had actually been like. Readers should remember that purpose. It is a loving book, and it chooses its material. But it is the fullest window we have into the world that made her, and nothing in the other sources contradicts its main lines.

Morning and Evening

The centre of the Howard household was family worship, and it happened twice a day, every day. In the morning, after breakfast and before anyone left for school or work, the family gathered. They sang a hymn, usually all its verses, and over the years the children learned scores of hymns by heart without ever setting out to memorise them. Their father read a passage of Scripture, and then he prayed. There were prayers again in the evening. Visitors, of whom there were many, were expected to join in, and most did.

The prayers were not vague. Philip Howard prayed for his children by name, for the work of the day, for the nation, and for missionaries all over the world, many of whom the family knew personally. The Sunday School Times put its editor in touch with Christian workers in many countries, and a steady stream of them passed through the Howard home, sat at its table, and told their stories. The Howard children grew up with the mission field not as a distant abstraction but as a matter of familiar faces, letters from far away, and answered and unanswered prayers. It is not surprising that several of them gave their lives to Christian service.

The children were also expected to learn Scripture by heart, and they did. The words of the King James Bible, and of the old hymns, sank into them early and stayed. Elisabeth Elliot’s later writing is shot through with the cadences of both, and in the hardest seasons of her life it was often a verse learned in childhood, or a line of a hymn, that came back to her when nothing else did.

Order and Obedience

The household ran on order. Meals were at fixed times, and the family ate together. The children had their tasks and were expected to do them without being reminded. Manners mattered: one sat up at table, waited to be served, did not interrupt, and wrote thank-you letters promptly. Obedience was expected the first time something was asked, and when it was not given there were consequences. Elisabeth later defended this kind of discipline firmly, and in a later age some readers found her defence of it severe. But the children of the house seem to have experienced it, on the whole, not as harshness but as security. They knew where the lines were, and they knew they were loved.

Sunday was set apart from the other days. The family went to church together, and the day was kept more quietly than the rest of the week. Here too the rule was not presented as a burden. It was simply the shape of the week, and the children grew up assuming that God had a claim on their time as well as on their hearts.

Katharine Howard was the practical engine of all this. She ran a large household on a small income, kept it clean and orderly, fed the family and its many guests, and set standards of courtesy and self-control that her children never quite escaped. She was capable and practical, and she expected a great deal. Philip Howard was gentler and quieter, a man of steady and unhurried faith, who loved the natural world and passed that love on to his children. Elisabeth was close to both of them, though in different ways, and she later wrote of both with deep gratitude and without pretending that either was perfect.

Franconia

Every summer the family went north to New Hampshire, to Gale Cottage, a house built by an earlier generation of the family in the village of Franconia, among the White Mountains. There, away from the city and the office, the children roamed the woods and fields, climbed the hills, swam in cold water, picked berries, and learned the names of trees, flowers and birds. Elisabeth loved it more than anywhere else. The mountains of New Hampshire gave her something she never lost: a delight in the physical world as God’s handiwork, and a need, all through her life, for quiet and for wild places. When she came back to the United States as a widow many years later, it was to Franconia that she went.

Six Children

It would be pleasant to report that a home like this produced six children who all walked the same path. The truth is more interesting. The Howard children were strong-minded, and they went in different directions. Philip, the eldest, became a missionary among the Slavey people of Canada’s Northwest Territories. David became a missionary in Latin America and later a leader in world missions. Thomas became a teacher of English and a writer of distinction, and in 1985 he left evangelicalism and became a Roman Catholic, a decision that grieved some of his family and that he explained with great care in his own books. Each of the six would have told the story of their childhood a little differently.

What they shared was a common inheritance: a deep familiarity with Scripture, a habit of prayer, a respect for words, and an assumption that life is lived before God and owes him obedience. Elisabeth took all of these with her. She also took with her some of the household’s reserve. The Howards were not demonstrative, and she grew up in a family where feelings were kept under control and not much discussed. That reserve would serve her well in some of the hardest moments of her life, and it would also, at times, make her seem distant to those who did not know her well.

The verse at the head of this chapter is Moses’ charge to Israel’s parents: to teach God’s words to their children when they sat in the house, walked by the way, lay down and rose up. Philip and Katharine Howard did exactly that, day after day, for more than twenty years. They could not make their children believe. But they gave them the words, and in Elisabeth’s case the words took root.

fields.title: Hampden DuBose
fields.body_html:
“Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.”

— Hebrews 12:11, KJV

A School in Florida

In 1941, when she was fourteen, Elisabeth Howard left home for a boarding school in Florida. The school was the Hampden DuBose Academy, a small Christian boarding school then in Orlando, which later moved a few miles north-west to Zellwood. It had been founded in 1934 by Dr Pierre W. DuBose and his wife, and it took its name from his father, Hampden Coit DuBose, a Southern Presbyterian who had spent most of his working life as a missionary in the city of Soochow in China.

The academy was a school with a missionary purpose. Many of its pupils were the children of missionaries serving overseas, and others came from Christian families who wanted an education in which faith was not an extra but the foundation. The school was small enough for everyone to know everyone else. Its days were structured from rising to lights-out: chapel, lessons, study hall, meals, work, recreation and evening vespers, each in its place. For a girl from the Howard household this was not entirely strange. But the school also had a character of its own, and it was stamped by the personality of the woman who ran it.

Mrs DuBose

Mrs DuBose was the headmistress, and by every account she was formidable. She was a Southern lady of the old school, with exacting standards of dress, deportment, speech and manners, and decided views about what a Christian young woman ought to be. She believed that good manners were a form of consideration for others, and that awkwardness and self-absorption were faults to be corrected rather than temperaments to be indulged. She did not hesitate to tell her pupils so.

Elisabeth arrived at the school tall, gawky, and so shy that she could barely speak to people she did not know. Mrs DuBose singled her out. Elisabeth, who later described herself as a tall and very shy girl of fourteen on arrival, remembered being told plainly that shyness was not a virtue to be indulged, and that she must learn to engage with other people. The girl was frightened of her headmistress. But she took the warning seriously, and she set herself to change.

It was not a gentle education, and some of what the school prized, the ladylike graces of the American South, the careful attention to appearances, may seem to a later age to have been of doubtful importance. But Elisabeth came to believe that Mrs DuBose had done her a great service. She had been made to understand that shyness, however painful, is a form of preoccupation with oneself, and that a Christian has a duty to look outward, to put others at their ease, and to do the uncomfortable thing that love requires. She learned to stand straight, to look people in the eye, to make conversation with strangers, to speak in public, and to carry herself with a composure that later observers often mistook for natural self-possession. It was not natural. It had been learned, at some cost, at Hampden DuBose.

She also learned something of the discipline of the inner life. The school expected its pupils to read the Bible and pray daily on their own, not merely to sit through chapel, and it expected them to think of their lives as belonging to God. Elisabeth seems to have taken all of this with the earnestness that marked her whole adolescence. She kept notebooks. She marked her Bible. She began to think seriously about what God might want her to do with her life.

A Spiritual Mother

The most lasting gift of Hampden DuBose, however, came through the evening vespers. Mrs DuBose was a great admirer of Amy Carmichael, the Irish missionary who had gone to South India in 1895 and founded the Dohnavur Fellowship, a community that rescued children in danger of being given to temple service and raised them as its own. By the 1940s Amy Carmichael had been an invalid for a decade, confined to her room after a fall, but she was still writing, and her books of devotion, poetry and missionary narrative were widely read. Mrs DuBose quoted from them often at vespers.

Elisabeth was captivated. She found in Amy Carmichael a voice unlike any she had heard: severe and tender at once, utterly without sentimentality, uncompromising about the cost of discipleship, and yet full of a kind of gaiety. Amy Carmichael wrote about the missionary life as it actually was, with its disappointments, its loneliness and its unglamorous daily duties, and she insisted that the love of Christ asks for everything. In her little book If, a series of searching tests of the heart, each of the short entries ends with the same refrain: “then I know nothing of Calvary love.” For a serious girl of fourteen, already wondering whether God might be calling her to the mission field, it was strong and heady reading.

Elisabeth later spoke of Amy Carmichael as her first spiritual mother, and the influence lasted for the rest of her life. More than forty years after those vespers she wrote a full-length biography of her, A Chance to Die, published in 1987. Some of the qualities readers most associated with Elisabeth Elliot, her suspicion of emotionalism in religion, her insistence on obedience whether or not one feels like it, her readiness to accept suffering as part of the Christian’s portion, and her plain, unadorned style, can be traced back in part to the books she first heard read aloud in a Florida chapel.

1944

Elisabeth stayed at Hampden DuBose for three years. They were the years of the Second World War. The United States entered the war in December 1941, a few months after she arrived, and by the time she graduated the war had reached into almost every American family. Florida filled with training camps and airfields. The war did not touch the school directly, but it gave an edge of seriousness to the talk of giving one’s life to God that she heard at chapel.

She graduated in 1944 with a changed manner. She was still reserved. She would always be reserved. But she had learned to master her shyness instead of being mastered by it, and she had begun to believe that God had work for her to do in the world. She had settled, too, on what that work might be. She wanted to translate the Bible into languages that had never had it, and for that she would need a thorough knowledge of the language in which the New Testament had been written. In the autumn she went to Wheaton College, in Illinois, to study Greek.

The verse at the head of this chapter speaks of discipline that seems grievous at the time and yields its fruit afterward. Elisabeth did not enjoy everything about Hampden DuBose, and she was frightened of its headmistress. But she lived to be grateful for both, and the fruit of those three years was visible in her for the rest of her life.

The school expected its pupils to read the Bible and pray daily on their own, not merely to sit through chapel, and it expected them to think of their lives as belonging to God. Elisabeth seems to have taken all of this with the earnestness that marked her whole adolescence. She kept notebooks. She marked her Bible. She began to think seriously about what God might want her to do with her life. A Spiritual Mother The most lasting gift of Hampden DuBose, however, came through the evening vespers. Mrs DuBose was a great admirer of Amy Carmichael, the Irish missionary who had gone to South India in 1895 and founded the Dohnavur Fellowship, a community that rescued children in danger of being given to temple service and raised them as its own. By the 1940s Amy Carmichael had been an invalid for a decade, confined to her room after a fall, but she was still writing, and her books of devotion, poetry and missionary narrative were widely read. Mrs DuBose quoted from them often at vespers. Elisabeth was captivated. She found in Amy Carmichael a voice unlike any she had heard: severe and tender at once, utterly without sentimentality, uncompromising about the cost of discipleship, and yet full of a kind of gaiety. Amy Carmichael wrote about the missionary life as it actually was, with its disappointments, its loneliness and its unglamorous daily duties, and she insisted that the love of Christ asks for everything. In her little book If, a series of searching tests of the heart, each of the short entries ends with the same refrain: “then I know nothing of Calvary love.” For a serious girl of fourteen, already wondering whether God might be calling her to the mission field, it was strong and heady reading. Elisabeth later spoke of Amy Carmichael as her first spiritual mother, and the influence lasted for the rest of her life. More than forty years after those vespers she wrote a full-length biography of her, A Chance to Die, published in 1987. Some of the qualities readers most associated with Elisabeth Elliot, her suspicion of emotionalism in religion, her insistence on obedience whether or not one feels like it, her readiness to accept suffering as part of the Christian’s portion, and her plain, unadorned style, can be traced back in part to the books she first heard read aloud in a Florida chapel. 1944 Elisabeth stayed at Hampden DuBose for three years. They were the years of the Second World War. The United States entered the war in December 1941, a few months after she arrived, and by the time she graduated the war had reached into almost every American family. Florida filled with training camps and airfields. The war did not touch the school directly, but it gave an edge of seriousness to the talk of giving one’s life to God that she heard at chapel. She graduated in 1944 with a changed manner. She was still reserved. She would always be reserved. But she had learned to master her shyness instead of being mastered by it, and she had begun to believe that God had work for her to do in the world. She had settled, too, on what that work might be. She wanted to translate the Bible into languages that had never had it, and for that she would need a thorough knowledge of the language in which the New Testament had been written. In the autumn she went to Wheaton College, in Illinois, to study Greek. The verse at the head of this chapter speaks of discipline that seems grievous at the time and yields its fruit afterward. Elisabeth did not enjoy everything about Hampden DuBose, and she was frightened of its headmistress. But she lived to be grateful for both, and the fruit of those three years was visible in her for the rest of her life.

fields.title: Greek at Wheaton
fields.body_html:
“Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.”

— 2 Timothy 2:15, KJV

A College on the Prairie

Wheaton College stands in the town of Wheaton, Illinois, some twenty-five miles west of Chicago, on what was once open prairie. It had been founded in 1860 under Jonathan Blanchard, an abolitionist and reformer, and by the 1940s it was perhaps the best-known evangelical liberal arts college in the United States. Its students signed a pledge of conduct, attended chapel daily, and were taught by a faculty committed to the authority of Scripture. Its president when Elisabeth Howard arrived in the autumn of 1944 was V. Raymond Edman, who had himself been a missionary in Ecuador in the 1920s, working among the Quichua of the Andean highlands until illness forced him home. No one could have known how much that country would come to mean to several of the students then passing through his chapel services.

The college Elisabeth entered was a wartime college. Many of the young men were away in the forces, and for a time women made up a large share of the student body. After the war ended in 1945 the veterans came back in numbers, older and more serious than ordinary undergraduates, many of them studying on government grants, and the campus grew crowded and lively. Through all of it the rhythms of the college went on: lectures, chapel, literary societies, prayer meetings, and the steady pressure of students who wanted to know what God was calling them to do.

Why Greek

Elisabeth chose to major in classical Greek. It was an unusual choice for a young woman in 1944, but she had a clear reason for it. She believed God was calling her to translate the Bible for a people who did not yet have it, and she wanted to be able to work from the original text of the New Testament rather than from an English version. The course was demanding. Students read Homer, the dramatists, the historians and Plato as well as the New Testament, and they learned the grammar thoroughly, by drill and repetition, in the old way.

Greek suited her. She had a precise mind, a good ear and the patience to work through difficult texts word by word. The discipline of translation, of finding exactly the right word in one language for a word in another, and of refusing to settle for a vague approximation, became part of her habit of thought. Those who later admired the clarity of her English prose were often admiring, without knowing it, the fruit of four years of Greek composition. She came to love the language for its own sake, and she kept her Greek New Testament close for the rest of her life.

She was, by the accounts of those who knew her at Wheaton, a serious and rather solitary student, more respected than popular. She was not unfriendly, but she was reserved, and she did not chase the social life of the campus. She was deeply concerned to know and do God’s will, and she prayed about it constantly. She had decided that she would rather remain single and serve God on the mission field than marry the wrong man, and she was quite prepared for that to be her lot.

Jim Elliot

In the autumn of 1945 a new student arrived from Portland, Oregon. Philip James Elliot, always called Jim, had been born there on 8 October 1927, the third of four children of Fred and Clara Elliot. His father preached in the small Plymouth Brethren assemblies to which the family belonged, and his mother was a chiropractor. Jim had grown up in a home as devout, in its own way, as the Howards’, and he had come to faith as a small boy. At high school he had already been a confident public speaker. At Wheaton he threw himself into everything. He joined the wrestling team and became one of its best members. He was active in the student missionary fellowship. And he, too, chose to study Greek.

Jim was a year younger than Elisabeth and a year behind her at college. He was handsome, athletic, outspoken and intense, with a strong sense of humour and a habit of saying exactly what he thought. He had very little time for what he regarded as frivolity, including much of the social life of the college, and he had decided views about the dangers of romantic entanglements for a young man who meant to serve God. He read the lives of missionaries and was moved above all by the diary of David Brainerd, the young American who had given his short life to preaching among the native peoples of New York, Pennsylvania and New Jersey in the 1740s, and who had died at twenty-nine. Brainerd’s single-minded devotion, and his willingness to be spent for God, became something of a pattern for Jim.

Jim’s closest friend at Wheaton was Elisabeth’s younger brother, David Howard, who wrestled alongside him and shared his missionary zeal. Elisabeth knew Jim by sight and by reputation, as one knows people at a small college. It was through Dave that she came to know him better.

Christmas in Moorestown

At Christmas 1947 Dave invited Jim home to Moorestown for the holidays. Jim stayed with the Howards, joined in the family prayers and hymn-singing, and talked late into the evenings. He seems to have felt at home in a household so like his own in its seriousness about God. It was in the weeks that followed that he began to notice Dave’s sister in a new way.

When the new term began in January 1948, Elisabeth and Jim found themselves in some of the same Greek classes, and they began to study together. They were both good at it, and both competitive. They talked about Greek, about the Bible, about missions and about the will of God. Jim had just begun to keep a journal, which would one day be published and read by hundreds of thousands, and he began, guardedly, to write about her in it. Elisabeth, for her part, kept her own counsel, and her own journal. Each was, in a sense, waiting to see what the other would do, and each was determined not to do anything that God had not plainly sanctioned.

She was a senior, and in June she would graduate. Neither of them knew what the spring would bring, or that it would begin a story that would occupy them for more than five years before it reached any resolution.

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s charge to Timothy to be a workman who handles the word of truth rightly. It was the verse that might have stood over Elisabeth’s Greek grammar. She went to Wheaton to learn to handle God’s word with care, so that she might one day give it to others in their own tongue. She learned that, and she learned something else besides, which she had not gone looking for.

fields.title: A Love Laid on the Altar
fields.body_html:
“I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.”

— Romans 12:1, KJV

Spring 1948

Through the early months of 1948 Elisabeth Howard and Jim Elliot studied Greek together, talked, and watched each other. At the end of April they went together to a large Christian gathering in Chicago, which was, by the standards of the time and the place, a date, though neither of them would have used the word lightly. As the spring went on, it became clear to both of them that something more than friendship was growing. It became equally clear that neither knew what to do about it.

For Elisabeth the difficulty was partly one of temperament. She had been brought up to believe that a woman did not reveal her feelings to a man until he had declared his, and she held to that conviction firmly. She was also reserved by nature, and anxious not to want anything that God had not given. Her private journals from these months, now drawn on by her biographer, show that the outward composure was not the whole story. She was in love, and she found the uncertainty very hard to bear.

For Jim the difficulty was one of conviction. He had come to believe, from his reading of Scripture, that God might be calling him to remain single for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He had taken very seriously Paul’s words in the seventh chapter of First Corinthians about the unmarried man caring for the things of the Lord, and Christ’s words about those who make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom’s sake. He thought that a missionary pioneer, going into hard and dangerous places, might be better without a wife, and he feared that marriage might divide his heart. He was not sure. But he was not willing to proceed until he was sure, and he was not willing to let his feelings decide the question for him.

A Walk in June

On 9 June, shortly before Elisabeth’s graduation, the two of them went for a walk in the evening, south of the campus, and came to a cemetery. There, by their own later accounts, they spoke openly for the first time of what each felt for the other. And Jim told her also that he believed God might be leading him to remain single, at least for now, and that he could not ask her for anything or promise her anything.

They agreed, in the end, to give the matter back to God. The image they both used, then and later, was of the altar. In the twenty-second chapter of Genesis, God asks Abraham to offer his son Isaac, the son of the promise, as a burnt offering on Mount Moriah. Abraham goes, builds the altar, binds Isaac and lays him on it, and only then does God provide a ram instead. Jim and Elisabeth understood their love in that light. It was a gift from God, and it was precious, and for that very reason it must be offered back to him without conditions. If God gave it back to them, well and good. If he did not, they would trust that he had something better.

As they sat there, they became aware that the moon, risen behind them, was throwing the shadow of a large stone cross between them. Both of them remembered it, and Elisabeth told of it years later. Neither treated it as a magical sign, but both took it as a picture of what they had just agreed: that the cross stood between them, and that whatever happened to their love would happen under it.

No Promises

Soon afterwards Elisabeth graduated and left Wheaton. Jim had another year to go. There was no engagement, and no understanding of the kind that young couples of the time often had. They did not regard themselves as committed to each other. They agreed to write, but even that was a matter of some scruple, and the letters that followed were frequent at some periods and sparse at others. Jim, especially, was careful not to say anything that would bind either of them. Elisabeth, for her part, held herself to her principle that a woman should wait for the man to lead, and she waited.

It is easy, three generations later, to find all this strange, and some readers find it painful. Two young people who loved each other deeply, and who both wanted to marry, chose to live for years with no promise at all, because one of them was not yet sure that marriage was God’s will for him. They saw each other only rarely. They went for long periods without knowing whether the story would end in marriage or in a lifetime of separate service. The waiting was hard, and Elisabeth’s private writings make clear that she sometimes found it almost unbearable. But neither of them ever suggested that they had been forced into it. They chose it, freely, because they believed that the will of God was worth more than their own happiness, and that if they sought his will first, their happiness would be safe in his hands.

Passion and Purity

Elisabeth Elliot told the story of these years in Passion and Purity, published in 1984, nearly thirty years after Jim’s death. She drew on her own journals and on his letters, and she wrote it for young Christians struggling with questions of love, sex and the will of God in a culture that had largely abandoned restraint. The book was very widely read, and for many young people it was a lifeline: a picture of a love that was passionate and also chaste, and a reminder that self-control is not the enemy of love but its servant.

Not every reader was persuaded. Some felt that the book made one couple’s unusual path into a pattern for everyone, and that readers took from it rules that Scripture does not lay down. Others found its assumptions about the roles of men and women in courtship too rigid. These criticisms deserve a hearing, and they belong to the wider discussion of her teaching, which the companion volume takes up. But the story itself, as a matter of history, is not in dispute. Jim and Elisabeth did what they said they did. They loved each other and laid that love on the altar, and they left it there for a long time.

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s appeal to the Romans to present their bodies as a living sacrifice. It is a hard word. It does not speak of a single dramatic offering but of a life laid down continually, day after day. That was the shape of the years that followed the walk in June 1948. The altar was not a moment. It was a place where they had to keep returning.

fields.title: The Waiting Years
fields.body_html:
“It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.”

— Lamentations 3:26, KJV

Three Hills

In the autumn of 1948 Elisabeth Howard went north to Canada, to the Prairie Bible Institute at Three Hills, Alberta. It was a long way from Moorestown in every sense. Three Hills was a small farming town on the open plains north-east of Calgary, bitterly cold in winter and remote at any season, and the institute was a large, plain, intensely disciplined Bible school founded in 1922 by L. E. Maxwell, an American who had come to the Canadian prairies as a young man. Maxwell was a preacher of the cross. His great theme was the believer’s union with Christ in his death, and the call to die daily to self. His students lived simply, worked hard, rose early, and were expected to take the cost of discipleship with complete seriousness. Many of them went on to the mission field, and the school sent out missionaries all over the world.

Elisabeth went to Prairie for a year of Bible study after her Greek degree, to prepare herself further for missionary work. The austerity of the place, and its stress on self-denial, suited the mood in which she had left Wheaton. She had laid her love on the altar, and she was determined to leave it there. The year was not easy. She was lonely and far from home, she did not know whether she would ever marry, and the letters from Jim, when they came, were careful and uncommitted. But she worked, and she prayed, and she later counted the year as part of her training.

After the year at the institute she stayed on in Alberta for a time, doing rural Sunday school work among the farms around the hamlet of Patience, and learning what it meant to work far from the support of family and friends. It was, in its way, an apprenticeship for what was to come.

Jim’s Road

Meanwhile Jim finished his studies at Wheaton and graduated in 1949. He went home to Portland and spent a good deal of the next two years there, working, studying the Bible, preaching in small churches and assemblies, and seeking God’s direction. He was impatient with what he saw as the complacency of American churches, and he was increasingly certain that God was calling him to pioneer missionary work, though for a long time he did not know where.

In the summer of 1950 Jim attended the Summer Institute of Linguistics at the University of Oklahoma in Norman, the training school run by Wycliffe Bible Translators. There he met people with experience of Ecuador, and he heard about the Quichua people of the eastern rainforest and about the Waorani, a people beyond them whom no outsider had yet reached in friendship. Within months he was convinced that God was sending him to Ecuador. He looked for a companion and found one in Pete Fleming, a gifted young man from Seattle with a master’s degree in literature, who after much prayer decided to go with him. The two of them prepared for more than a year. On 4 February 1952 they sailed from San Pedro, California, and they reached Ecuador later that month.

None of this made things simpler for Elisabeth. Jim was still not sure about marriage, and he still said so. For a time he seemed to lean towards it and then away again. The two of them met only a handful of times in the four years after Wheaton, and their meetings were often brief and sometimes painful. Their letters, many of which their daughter later published in Devotedly, show two people who loved each other and were trying hard to be honest with God and with each other, and who did not always succeed in understanding each other. There were misunderstandings and silences.

A Call of Her Own

Through these years Elisabeth held on to the conviction she had formed at Hampden DuBose and at Wheaton: that God had called her to translate the Scriptures for a people who did not have them. She took the course of the Summer Institute of Linguistics, learning how to analyse the sounds and structure of an unwritten language, how to devise an alphabet for it, and how to begin the slow work of grammar and dictionary from nothing. She was good at it. Her ear and her training in Greek gave her a head start, and she found that the work suited her careful, methodical mind.

The question was where to go. In the end she settled on Ecuador, where there were peoples whose languages had never been written down, and where missionaries already at work were glad of a trained linguist. It is natural to wonder whether she would have chosen Ecuador if Jim had not been going there. The sources do not settle the question, and it may be that she could not have settled it herself. What is clear is that she went with no promise from Jim, no engagement and no understanding, and that she went to do work of her own, independently, as a single missionary. fields.title: San Miguel de los Colorados
fields.body_html:
“And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?”

— Acts 2:8, KJV

Quito

Quito in 1952 was a city of perhaps two hundred thousand people, built in a long valley more than nine thousand feet up in the Andes, ringed by volcanoes and some fifteen miles south of the equator. Its old centre was a maze of steep cobbled streets, whitewashed walls and colonial churches heavy with gold. The air was thin and the sun was fierce, and newcomers from sea level were short of breath for weeks. For a missionary arriving in Ecuador it was the natural place to begin. The government offices were there, the mission headquarters were there, and above all the language schools and teachers were there.

Elisabeth Howard spent her first months in Ecuador in Quito, learning Spanish. It was not the language of the people she had come to serve, but it was the language of the country, of its officials and landowners and traders, and of most of the people she would meet on the edges of the forest. Without it she could not do anything. She worked at it with her usual thoroughness, and her training in languages made the work easier than it was for many. Jim Elliot and Pete Fleming were in the city at the same time, doing the same thing, and the small missionary community of Quito saw a good deal of the three young Americans. Then, after some months, she left the capital and went west; by the autumn of 1952 she was writing home from the western forest.

The Western Forest

The Andes divide Ecuador into three worlds. In the middle are the high mountain valleys where most of the people then lived. To the east the land falls away into the vast rainforest of the Amazon basin, where Jim was going. To the west it falls, just as steeply, towards the Pacific coast, and on that western slope, below the clouds, there was in those years a belt of dense, wet, tropical forest, cut by rivers and only beginning to be cleared for farms and plantations. A rough road wound down from the mountains into it. At the bottom, many hours’ hard travel from Quito, was the small frontier town of Santo Domingo de los Colorados, and not far from it a scattering of clearings and houses called San Miguel de los Colorados.

The names come from the people who lived there. The Spanish called them the Colorados, the red ones, because the men dyed their hair a brilliant red with the paste of the achiote seed and moulded it into a stiff, close cap on their heads. They painted their bodies with black stripes and wore striped cloths about their waists. They call themselves the Tsáchila, and their language is now known as Tsafiki. In 1952 they were a small people, living in houses scattered through the forest rather than in villages, farming their clearings, fishing and hunting. They had been in contact with outsiders for a long time. Their land was being encroached on by settlers from the highlands, and they were wary of strangers. Their language had never been written down.

That was why Elisabeth had come. Three other single women missionaries were working from San Miguel, and she joined them as the linguist of the team. Her task, as she understood it, was to learn the Colorado language from the beginning, to work out its sounds and devise an alphabet, to analyse its grammar, and to lay the foundations for a translation of the Scriptures into it. It was exactly the work for which she had spent eight years preparing, and she went to it with high hopes.

Learning from Nothing

There was no grammar to study, no dictionary to consult and no teacher to explain. The method she had been taught was to begin with the simplest things: to point to an object and write down, as exactly as she could, what was said; to listen to the same word over and over until she could hear its sounds; to record everything in a phonetic script, on slips and cards that could be sorted and resorted; and slowly to build from words to phrases, from phrases to sentences, and from sentences to the patterns underneath. It was meticulous, repetitive and exhausting work. Every guess had to be tested. Every rule had exceptions. Progress was measured in days and weeks, not in hours, and a single misheard sound could lead a whole set of notes astray.

The conditions did not help. It rained a great deal, and the heat and the damp got into everything. There were insects, snakes and mud. The missionaries lived simply in a plain house, and the life was hard on the body and harder on the spirit. The Colorados were courteous but mostly uninterested in what the foreign women had come to say. Relations between Protestant and Roman Catholic missionaries in Ecuador at that time were often tense, and that tension, too, was part of the life of the frontier.

What she needed above all was an informant: a person who spoke the language natively, who could also speak Spanish well enough to explain what the words meant, and who had the patience to sit with a foreigner for hours on end repeating things. Without such a person the work could not go forward. Finding one was not easy. The Colorados who knew Spanish well were few, and those who did had their own work and little reason to spend it with a missionary.

A Death in the Forest

During her months at San Miguel, Elisabeth met the first of the losses that would mark her year there. By her later account, a Colorado woman went into a hard labour, and Elisabeth was there. She was not a nurse, and no doctor was within reach. What help could be given was given, and it was not enough. The woman died.

Elisabeth was shaken to the roots. She had come to Ecuador believing that God had sent her, and that he would bless the work she did in obedience to him. Now she had done her best, in obedience, and a young woman was dead. She did not know what to say to the woman’s family, or to God. More than twenty years later, when she came to write about that first year, she did not pretend that she had understood it at the time, or that she understood it fully even then.

The verse at the head of this chapter is the astonished question of the crowd on the day of Pentecost, when they heard the apostles speak the wonderful works of God, every man in his own language. It is the vision behind all Bible translation: that God means to be heard by every people in the tongue in which they were born. Elisabeth went to San Miguel to serve that vision. She had no idea how much it would cost her, or how little, in the end, she would have to show for it.

fields.title: Macario, and a Stolen Suitcase
fields.body_html:
“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.”

— Isaiah 55:8-9, KJV

Don Macario

The informant Elisabeth Howard needed came to her in the person of a man named Macario, to whom she gave, as Ecuadorians did, the courtesy title of Don. Accounts of him differ in detail. By her own account he had grown up on a hacienda alongside Colorado children, and he spoke both Colorado and Spanish with complete ease. That alone made him precious, for people who could move freely between the two languages were very few. But he was more than a bilingual speaker. He was, by her account, a believer in Christ, intelligent and patient, and he was willing to give his time to the work. Elisabeth could hardly have hoped for anyone better.

With Macario at her side the work began to move. Day after day they sat together while she asked and he answered, and she wrote down, tested, sorted and wrote again. Words became lists, lists became patterns, and the patterns began to show the shape of the language underneath. The cards multiplied. She began to see how the sounds of Colorado could be represented in an alphabet that its own speakers might one day learn to read. She began to work out how its verbs were built and how its sentences were put together. After months of slow and lonely labour, it must have seemed that God was at last confirming the call that had brought her to Ecuador.

A Shot in the Forest

Then Macario was killed. By the account usually given, he was clearing a piece of land he regarded as his own when a group of men arrived and claimed it for one of them; when he refused to give way, he was shot dead. Disputes over land were common on the forest frontier, where settlers from the highlands were pressing in and titles were uncertain, and they were sometimes settled with violence.

The man who had been the key to all her work, and a brother in Christ, had been murdered in a quarrel about a few acres of forest, and there was nothing to be done. There was no one to take his place. The few others who knew both languages could not or would not do what he had done, and the work that had been moving so hopefully came to a halt.

She did not understand it. She had prayed for an informant, and God had given her one, and now God had allowed him to be taken away in the most senseless manner imaginable. She was young, she had given up a great deal to come to Ecuador, and she had done nothing, as far as she could see, but try to obey. If obedience did not guarantee results, what did it guarantee? She asked the question honestly, and she did not find a quick answer.

Another Direction

In the midst of these months her life turned in another direction altogether. In January 1953, in Quito, Jim Elliot at last asked her to marry him, and she accepted. The story of the engagement, and of the condition Jim attached to it, belongs to the next chapter. Its immediate consequence was that Elisabeth would leave San Miguel and the Colorado work and go east, to the other side of the Andes and a different people. The work she had begun in the western forest would have to be left for others to take up, and the fruit of her labour there would be all she could hand on to them.

That fruit was on paper: the notebooks, the files of cards, the charts of sounds and forms, the beginnings of an alphabet and a grammar. It represented the greater part of her months of work, and all that remained of Macario’s patient help. She packed it into a suitcase so that it could go on to the colleagues who would carry the work forward, and, as far as the accounts tell, there were no copies.

She never saw it again. Word reached her, by letter, that the suitcase had been stolen from the back of a truck on its way. Whoever took it can have found nothing of value to them in it. Nothing was ever recovered. In a moment, almost everything she had to show for her time among the Colorados was gone.

These Strange Ashes

Elisabeth Elliot did not write about her year at San Miguel until more than twenty years later. When she did, in These Strange Ashes, published in 1975, she took her title from a poem by Amy Carmichael, the missionary whose books she had first heard read at Hampden DuBose. The poem asks God about the ashes left when an offering has been burnt, the nothingness and “this baffling sense of loss”, and answers by pointing to Christ’s own stripping on the cross, and to ashes as simply what follows when fire falls on a burnt offering. The book tells the story of the year plainly, without heroics and without a tidy ending: the woman who died in childbirth, the murder of Macario, the theft of the suitcase, and the questions they raised.

It was a brave book to publish. By 1975 Elisabeth Elliot was a well-known Christian author and speaker, and many of her readers knew her as the widow who had told the story of 1956 as a story of faith triumphant. Here she wrote, instead, about a year in which she had done what she believed God wanted and had nothing to show for it, and in which God had not explained himself. She did not claim that she had later discovered the hidden reasons. She concluded, rather, that the reasons were God’s business, and that the question she had to answer was not why God had done what he did, but whether she would go on trusting him without an explanation. The losses at San Miguel taught her, earlier than most Christians have to learn it, that faith which depends on visible success is not yet faith. Many readers, facing losses of their own that made no sense, have found the book a greater help than any success story.

Her first year as a missionary, then, ended in what looked like failure. She had not translated any Scripture. Her informant was dead, and her work was lost. She was twenty-six, newly engaged, and about to begin again from nothing, with a new language and a new people. It was not the last time that God would take from her the thing on which she had built her hopes, and it was perhaps a preparation for what was to come.

The verse at the head of this chapter is God’s word through Isaiah that his thoughts are not our thoughts, nor his ways our ways. It is not an explanation. It is a reminder that no explanation is owed. Elisabeth Howard learned in the western forest to live by that word, and she would need it, in the years ahead, more than she could possibly have imagined.

fields.title: Quichua First
fields.body_html:
“Whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.”

— Ruth 1:16, KJV

Quito, January 1953

Late in January 1953 Jim Elliot came up from the eastern forest to Quito, and Elisabeth came up from the western forest to meet him there. For five years their friendship had moved by inches. There had been the long letters, the careful silences, the meetings that ended without anything being said, and Jim’s repeated conviction that he must not ask her for anything until he was sure that God was not calling him to stay single. She had learned to live with that uncertainty, and to work hard while she lived with it.

In Quito Jim asked her to marry him, and she said yes. It was the end of a long road for both of them, and those who later read the letters of those years, edited by their daughter, have been struck by how little either of them presumed on it. Neither treated the engagement as God’s reward for having waited. They treated it as a new piece of obedience, with its own costs.

The first of those costs became clear almost at once. Jim did not want them to marry quickly. He was committed to the Quichua people of the eastern forest, the lowland speakers of a language related to the Quechua of the Andes, and he believed that a wife who could not speak to them would be of little use to the work and would be lonely in it. He asked Elisabeth to learn Quichua first. Only when she could speak it would they set a date.

The Condition

Many readers, meeting this condition for the first time, have found it hard. A man who had kept a woman waiting for five years now asked her to wait again, and to spend the waiting learning a language that was not the one she had come to Ecuador to study. It is fair to say that the arrangement suited Jim’s plans more than hers, and that it reflected his strong, sometimes impatient single-mindedness. It is also fair to say that she agreed to it freely, and that she never afterwards described it as a grievance. She was a trained linguist. She knew better than he did how long it takes to learn a language well, and how easily a missionary can live for years among a people while understanding very little of what they say. If she was to share his work, she wanted to share it properly.

Agreeing to Jim’s condition meant leaving San Miguel. The previous chapter has told how her months among the Colorado people ended in loss. It is enough to say here that she went east into a new language and a new people knowing that the same thing could happen again, and that the Colorado work was left to the colleagues who stayed.

Lowland Quichua was a different proposition from Colorado. It was not an unwritten language in quite the same sense. Missionaries and Catholic priests had worked with Quechua speakers for centuries, and there were word lists, some grammar and some Scripture in the highland forms of the language. But the forest dialect of the Napo region had its own sounds and words, and much of what had been written did not fit it. A learner had to listen, write down what she heard, test it on the people, and correct herself again and again. Elisabeth had been trained to do exactly that. Early in the summer of 1953 she moved to the mission station at Dos Ríos, in the eastern forest, worked with Quichua helpers there, and set about making the language her own.

The sources do not record every move she made in these months, and this book does not try to supply them. What is clear is that she spent the rest of 1953 in the eastern forest among the Quichua, with other missionaries close by and with Jim sometimes near and often not. He was busy. Shandia, the station he and Pete Fleming had taken over, was largely swept away when the river beside it flooded in the summer of 1953, and the months that followed went into rebuilding and into the school and the preaching that the Shandia believers depended on. Ed McCully and his wife Marilou had also joined the Quichua work, and the small team of young missionaries was stretched thin.

Her letters from these months, published long afterwards, show her doing what she did all her life: working steadily, observing closely, and recording her own failures without self-pity. She learned the language quickly by most standards. That did not make the learning easy. Every new word cost her hours of listening, and she was learning it in heat and damp, often unwell, among people whose ways she was only beginning to understand. She seems also to have been learning something about herself. For years she had been the one waiting for Jim to decide. Now the timing of the marriage depended largely on her own diligence, and she could not afford to coast.

What She Was Choosing

It would be easy to tell the story of 1953 as a romantic interlude, a year of waiting before a wedding. It was more serious than that. In accepting Jim’s condition, Elisabeth was choosing not only a husband but a people and a place, and a way of life that she knew would be hard. She was choosing to put aside, at least for a time, the work she had trained for, the translation of an unwritten language from nothing, and to give herself to work in which others had already broken the ground. She was choosing to live in the forest rather than in the town, among people she had not chosen, in the service of a calling that had first been his.

She did not do so as a woman without convictions of her own. She had come to Ecuador independently. She had worked as a single missionary, and she would remain, all her life, sharply resistant to the idea that a woman’s faith was merely an appendage of her husband’s. But she also believed that God led through ordinary circumstances, including the circumstance of loving a particular man, and that a choice freely made could be a way of obeying him. She did not think the two convictions were in conflict.

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from the book of Ruth. Ruth was a widow from Moab who refused to leave her mother-in-law, and who went with her to a country she did not know. Her words have often been read at weddings, though they were spoken by one woman to another, and spoken in grief. They suit this chapter in both senses. In 1953 Elisabeth Howard was learning to say to a people, as well as to a man, that their people would be hers. She could not know that within three years she would be a widow herself, and that she would have to decide again, alone, whether she meant it.
