fields.title: 8 October 1953
fields.body_html:
“Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.”

— Ecclesiastes 4:9, KJV

A Wedding Without Fuss

By the autumn of 1953 Elisabeth had learned enough Quichua to satisfy Jim, and they set the date. They were married in Quito on Thursday 8 October 1953, which was Jim’s twenty-sixth birthday. It was a civil ceremony, conducted in Spanish at the government registry office, as Ecuadorian law required of every marriage. There was no church service afterwards, no procession and no reception of the kind their families at home might have expected. A handful of friends from the missionary community in Quito were present, and the whole affair was brief.

Some who hear this for the first time assume that the young couple were too poor or too remote to do anything more. That was not the reason. Both of them disliked show, and Jim in particular seems to have had little patience with what he saw as the fuss of the conventional church wedding. He had grown up among the Brethren in Portland, where ceremony was distrusted. Elisabeth, for her part, had been raised in a home where family worship mattered far more than occasions, and she seems to have been content. Whatever others thought, the two people most concerned were satisfied that they had been married before God and the law, and that nothing essential had been left out.

Their families were thousands of miles away and could not be there. Letters went north to Moorestown and to Portland. Both families learned of the wedding at a distance, as missionary families of that generation often did, and had to be content with letters and, later, photographs.

Panama

After the wedding they went away together for a short honeymoon, travelling north to Panama. Some accounts add a few days in Costa Rica. It was brief. By the late autumn they were back in Ecuador and on their way east to the forest.

It is worth pausing on what they brought to the marriage. Jim was intense, energetic and outspoken, a gifted preacher, a wrestler at college, a man who loved the outdoors and could be impatient with people who did not share his urgency. He was also warm, funny and deeply affectionate, and his journals show a man who could be very hard on himself. Elisabeth was more reserved, more analytical, and more inclined to see the difficulties in any plan. She had a sharp wit and could be blunt, and she was not afraid to disagree with him. Friends who knew them both have described a marriage of real affection and real equality of mind, if not of temperament. Each sharpened the other. Each sometimes exasperated the other. Neither was the plaster saint that the later legend made of them.

Elisabeth herself, many years later, was firm on this point. In her books and talks she discouraged readers from imagining that she and Jim had enjoyed a perfect marriage, or that their love story was a pattern that God would simply repeat for anyone who waited long enough. She had been married to Jim for twenty-seven months. They had been, by her account, happy months, but they had been ordinary ones too, full of the small irritations and adjustments of two strong-willed people learning to live in one small house.

The First Home

That small house was not yet built. When they reached the eastern forest at the end of 1953, the Shandia station was still being rebuilt after the flood, and the newly married Elliots did not move straight into it. Instead they went to Puyupungu, a Quichua settlement to the south of Shandia, where a local headman named Atanasio had asked for a missionary to teach his people and to start a school for their children. The Elliots set up house in a tent while a simple building was put up. It was an unpromising start to married life. The forest was wet, the insects were relentless, and every meal had to be cooked over a fire or on a small stove. They seem to have enjoyed it.

At Puyupungu Elisabeth had her first real test as a speaker of Quichua. The work was not hers alone or even mainly hers. Jim preached, taught and organised the school; she looked after the household, helped with simple medical care, and worked on the language. But she now had to use what she had learned, every day, in front of people who would laugh at her mistakes, and she did. The months of study in 1953 had not been wasted.

The Puyupungu arrangement did not last long. In June 1954 Pete Fleming married Olive Ainslie, the girl he had left behind in Seattle, and after a period of language study the new couple took up the work at Puyupungu. The Elliots moved back north to Shandia, where Jim built them a house on the rebuilt station. Shandia was to be their home for the rest of their married life.

Two Are Better

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from Ecclesiastes. The Preacher, who distrusts nearly every human achievement, makes an exception for companionship. Two are better than one, he says, because they have a good reward for their labour. It is a modest verse and an unromantic one. It makes no promises about feelings. It simply observes, as the next verse goes on to say, that if one falls the other can lift him up: work is easier, and burdens lighter, when they are shared.

Their gifts fitted together in just that way. Jim had picked up Quichua largely by ear and by use, talking with the schoolboys and the men of Shandia, and he spoke it with an ease that people warmed to. Elisabeth came to it as a trained linguist, listening for the patterns beneath the words, and she was better placed than he was to write it down, to teach others to read it, and in time to put Scripture into it. He was the preacher; she was the one with the notebook. Neither could have done the other’s work as well, and both knew it. The partnership was not always smooth, but it was a real one.

That was the shape of the Elliots’ marriage. They did not marry in order to be happy, though they were. They married in order to do together a work that each had already committed to doing alone, and they believed that God had joined them for that purpose. The marriage that began in a registry office in Quito, with no music and no flowers, was a working partnership as much as a love match, and it was both. Elisabeth would spend much of the rest of her life insisting that these were not opposites, and that obedience and affection, rightly ordered, belonged together. She had learned it in Ecuador, in a tent at Puyupungu, in the first year of being married to Jim.

fields.title: Shandia
fields.body_html:
“How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?”

— Romans 10:14, KJV

A Station in the Forest

Shandia lay in the forest of the upper Napo, on the eastern side of the Andes, among the Quichua people whose language Elisabeth had spent 1953 learning. It had been begun some years earlier by an older British missionary, Dr Wilfred Tidmarsh, and Jim and Pete Fleming had come to it in 1952 to carry the work on. In the summer of 1953 disaster struck, when the river rose and carried away much of the station. By the time the Elliots settled there as a married couple in 1954, the buildings had been put back on higher ground, and Jim had built a house for his wife.

Life at Shandia was simple by American standards and comfortable by the standards of the forest. There was a house with a roof that kept out the rain, a kitchen, a short-wave radio for the daily contact with the other stations, and, not far off, the small plane flown by the missionary pilot Nate Saint from his base at Shell Mera on the edge of the mountains, which was the station’s quickest link with the outside world. Supplies came by air or on the backs of carriers. The nearest town was a long walk away. The forest pressed close on every side, and the river was both the road and the danger.

The heart of the station was the school. Jim had inherited from Tidmarsh a school for Quichua boys, and he gave a great deal of himself to it. He taught reading and the Bible, and spent hours simply talking with the boys and their fathers. Out of the school came the first members of a small Quichua church. Jim preached in Quichua on Sundays and at other times through the week, and by the time of his death there was a group of young believers at Shandia who met together, prayed and read what Scripture they had in their own language. Some of them would carry on the work after he was gone.

Her Share of the Work

Elisabeth’s share of the work was less visible and, in the long run, perhaps as important. She ran the household, and in the forest that alone was a heavy task. She gave simple medical care to the people who came to the house with fevers, wounds, snakebites and infections, and she learned, as every missionary wife in such places learned, to act as nurse and sometimes as midwife with very little training. She taught women and girls. Above all she worked on the language. As a linguist she was better equipped than anyone else on the team to analyse Quichua, to prepare reading materials, and to work on the translation of portions of the New Testament. How much of it lasted is hard to say; like most first efforts of its kind, it was the sort of work that later translators build on, revise and sometimes replace.

It was not glamorous work, and she did not pretend it was. Her later books are full of plain descriptions of the routine of missionary life: the endless small tasks, the repetitions, the times when nothing seemed to be happening at all. She had come to the mission field with a picture of what it would be like, and the reality was more tedious and more ordinary than the picture. She learned at Shandia a lesson she would teach for the rest of her life, that faithfulness is mostly made up of the unremarkable duty that lies to hand, done well and offered to God, whether or not anyone notices.

Valerie

On 27 February 1955 the Elliots’ only child was born, a daughter, whom they named Valerie. Jim was delighted with her, and the letters and photographs of that year show a proud and affectionate father. For Elisabeth, motherhood in the forest added a new layer of work and a new kind of anxiety. There were few doctors and no hospitals near at hand, and the illnesses that came and went among the Quichua children could be deadly. She and Jim did what other missionary parents did. They took sensible precautions, prayed, and accepted that they could not control everything.

Valerie was ten months old when her father was killed. She was far too young to remember him, and she came to know him through her mother’s memories, through his journals and letters, and through the people who had known him. In her later years she edited and published her parents’ letters, which has given readers a much fuller picture of the marriage than the earlier books allowed.

The People Beyond the River

From his first months in Ecuador, Jim had heard about another people. To the south and east of the Quichua country, between the Napo and the Curaray rivers, lived a small and isolated group whom the Quichua feared. They had no contact with the outside world except through violence. Over the previous decades they had killed outsiders who came into their territory, including rubber workers, settlers and, in the 1940s, men working for the Shell oil company. They had killed Quichua as well. They also killed one another: later research suggests that a large share of the deaths among them were the result of spearings in long-running feuds. Outsiders called them by a Quichua word meaning savages. Their own name for themselves was Waorani, which means simply the people.

Jim was drawn to them almost from the beginning. He had long believed that his calling was to go where no one had gone with the gospel, and here was a people who had never heard it. Ed McCully, who had moved with Marilou to an old oil company base at Arajuno, on the edge of Waorani country, shared his interest, and so did Nate Saint. The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s question to the church at Rome: how shall they hear without a preacher? It was a question these young men took personally.

Elisabeth knew how Jim felt, and she knew what the risks were. In her own account she does not pretend that she was indifferent to them or that she found them easy to accept. But she did not try to dissuade him. She believed, as he did, that the Waorani needed to hear of Christ, and she had married a man whose readiness to go was part of what she loved in him. She had also learned at San Miguel that God did not promise success or safety to those who served him. In September 1955, when Nate Saint and Ed McCully, flying over the forest, finally spotted a cluster of Waorani houses, the decision that would change her life had, in a sense, already been made.

Outsiders called them by a Quichua word meaning savages. Their own name for themselves was Waorani, which means simply the people. Jim was drawn to them almost from the beginning. He had long believed that his calling was to go where no one had gone with the gospel, and here was a people who had never heard it. Ed McCully, who had moved with Marilou to an old oil company base at Arajuno, on the edge of Waorani country, shared his interest, and so did Nate Saint. The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s question to the church at Rome: how shall they hear without a preacher? It was a question these young men took personally. Elisabeth knew how Jim felt, and she knew what the risks were. In her own account she does not pretend that she was indifferent to them or that she found them easy to accept. But she did not try to dissuade him. She believed, as he did, that the Waorani needed to hear of Christ, and she had married a man whose readiness to go was part of what she loved in him. She had also learned at San Miguel that God did not promise success or safety to those who served him. In September 1955, when Nate Saint and Ed McCully, flying over the forest, finally spotted a cluster of Waorani houses, the decision that would change her life had, in a sense, already been made.

fields.title: Palm Beach
fields.body_html:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.”

— John 12:24, KJV

The Gift Drops

Five men took part in the attempt to reach the Waorani. Jim Elliot and Pete Fleming were working among the Quichua. Ed McCully was at Arajuno, the nearest station to Waorani country. Roger Youderian, a former army paratrooper who had fought in the Second World War, was working among the Shuar people in the south-east. Nate Saint, the pilot of Mission Aviation Fellowship, flew for all of them from Shell Mera. Each of the five was married, and four of them had young children. The name they gave the plan, Operation Auca, used the Quichua word for savage that was then the only name most outsiders had for the Waorani, a word the Waorani have rightly resented.

After the first sighting of Waorani houses in September 1955, the men began a programme of gift drops. Nate had worked out a way of lowering a bucket on a long line from a plane flying in tight circles, so that it hung almost still over a single spot on the ground. Week after week, from early October, he and Ed, and later the others, flew over the houses and let down machetes, cooking pots, cloth, beads and other gifts. They shouted phrases in the Waorani language through a loudspeaker. Jim had learned the phrases from Dayuma, a young Waorani woman who had fled her people some years before and was working on a hacienda in the foothills; it later became clear that they had been learned imperfectly. After a while the Waorani began to tie gifts of their own to the line: a feathered headband, food and other small things. To the men in the plane it looked like friendship.

They kept the plan almost entirely secret. They were afraid that publicity would bring others, the government or the press into Waorani country and wreck any chance of a peaceful contact, and they did not want to be talked out of it. Their wives knew. Most of their colleagues did not. Rachel Saint, Nate’s sister, who was learning the language from Dayuma at the hacienda, was not told. The secrecy has been questioned since, by historians and by some who knew the men, as has the speed with which the plan went forward. At the time, it seemed to the men the only way to proceed.

The Sandbar

On Tuesday 3 January 1956 Nate landed the plane on a sandbar on the Curaray river, a few miles from the Waorani houses, and over several flights brought in Jim, Ed and Roger with their supplies. The men built a shelter in a tree above the beach and called the place Palm Beach. Pete flew in and out with Nate, and at first the two of them spent their nights at Arajuno. For three days the men waited, called out their phrases towards the forest, and saw no one.

On Friday 6 January three Waorani came out on the far bank of the river: a young man, a young woman, and an older woman. They waded across and spent most of the day with the missionaries. They were given gifts and food, and the men photographed them. The young man was taken up in the plane and flown over the houses of his own people. The missionaries gave him and the young woman nicknames. Years later their names became known: the young man was Nenkiwi, the young woman Gimari, and the older woman Mintaka, who will appear again in this story. Towards evening the visitors drifted away. The older woman seems to have stayed on the beach after the others had gone. The men were elated. On Saturday no one came.

Sunday 8 January

On the morning of Sunday 8 January, Nate flew over the Waorani settlement and saw what he took to be a group of men walking towards the beach. Shortly after noon he spoke by radio to his wife Marj at Shell Mera, told her they expected visitors that afternoon, and promised to call again at half past four. When that time came, the radio from Palm Beach was silent. It never spoke again.

What happened that afternoon could only be pieced together years later, from the testimony of Waorani who were there, and the accounts do not agree in every particular. The outline is reasonably clear. Nenkiwi had gone off with Gimari without the older woman who should have accompanied them, and to deflect anger from himself he told his kinsmen that the foreigners had attacked them. The Waorani already believed that outsiders were dangerous, and some believed they ate people. A group of men, led by an older warrior named Gikita, decided to kill the strangers. Among them were Kimo, Mincaye, Dyuwi and Nampa, a brother of Dayuma. While women showed themselves across the river to draw the missionaries’ attention, the men came at them with spears.

The five had guns, and they had agreed beforehand that they would not use them against the Waorani. Most accounts say that shots were fired, but into the air or to frighten, not to kill. It seems that one bullet struck Nampa, probably by accident; whether that wound contributed to his death some time later is disputed. The precise order of events, who was speared first, and whether any of the five tried to reach the radio or the plane, cannot now be known with certainty, and this book does not try to reconstruct it. Nate Saint’s watch was later found stopped at a little after three o’clock. All five men died on the beach or in the river. The Waorani tore the fabric from the plane and went home.

No Fool

Six years earlier, a few months after leaving Wheaton, Jim Elliot had written in his journal on 28 October 1949 a sentence that has since been quoted more often than anything else he wrote: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” He had written it as a young man testing his own heart, not as an epitaph. Elisabeth later made it known to the world, and it has been printed on posters and bookmarks and in sermons ever since. It is worth reading it in the light of what actually happened, rather than in the glow of the legend. Jim did not know, when he wrote it, that he would die young, and on the sandbar he did not expect to die at all. The five men went in hope, not in search of martyrdom. What the sentence describes is not a plan for dying but a settled choice about what to hold loosely.

The verse at the head of this chapter is Christ’s own word about his death. A grain of wheat that is not buried remains a single grain; buried, it bears much fruit. The five men had read it many times. On the afternoon of 8 January 1956 they became, without choosing the hour or the manner, an instance of it. Whether the fruit would come, and what shape it would take, was hidden from everyone who waited that evening by the silent radios at Shell Mera and Arajuno. It was hidden most of all from Elisabeth.

fields.title: The Widow at Shandia
fields.body_html:
“A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.”

— Psalm 68:5, KJV

The Waiting

On the evening of Sunday 8 January 1956 the silence from Palm Beach could still be explained. Radios failed in the forest, batteries ran down, men forgot the time. By Monday morning it could not. Johnny Keenan, the other Mission Aviation Fellowship pilot in Ecuador, flew out over the Curaray and found the little yellow plane on the sandbar with its fabric stripped away. There was no sign of the men. The news went out on the missionary radio network, and the wives gathered at Shell Mera to wait.

The days that followed have been told many times, by Elisabeth among others, and the details need not be repeated at length here. A ground party set out overland towards the Curaray, led by Frank Drown, a missionary colleague of Roger Youderian’s, with other missionaries, Quichua men and Ecuadorian soldiers. The United States military sent aircraft and helicopters from the Panama Canal Zone to help. As the week went on, the bodies of four of the men were found in the river near the beach and identified, by their watches, wedding rings and other belongings. A fifth body, almost certainly Ed McCully’s, had been seen and examined earlier by a party of Quichua further downstream, but it could not afterwards be recovered. Late in the week the search party buried the four men together in a single grave at the edge of the beach, below the house in the tree, in the middle of a violent rainstorm, and then withdrew in haste, afraid of being attacked themselves.

The wives stayed at Shell Mera through it all. They cooked for the searchers, listened to the radio, looked after their children and waited for confirmation of what most of them already believed. When it came, the reports of those who were present agree that they received it with a composure that astonished the outsiders. Among those outsiders was the photographer Cornell Capa, who had flown in on assignment for Life magazine and who went out with the search party. His photographs, published later that month, showed the world the five widows and their children, and made their faces famous.

What Composure Meant

It is important to be careful here. The widows’ calm was real, and it came from a real faith. But it was later turned into something it was not: a picture of women who did not grieve, or who grieved less than others because they believed more. Elisabeth spent much of her later life correcting that impression. She did grieve, deeply and for a long time. She knew loneliness, exhaustion and fear. She had questions that were not answered. What she did not do was conclude that God had failed or abandoned her, and in that sense her calm was not an absence of grief but a decision about where to take it.

She was twenty-nine. Valerie was ten months old. Elisabeth had been married to Jim for a little over two years, and it was eight years since the winter at Wheaton when they had begun to study Greek together. She had no husband, no settled income beyond what friends and churches at home chose to send, and no obligation to stay in Ecuador. Most people expected her to go home.

Back to Shandia

She went back to Shandia. Before long she had returned, with Valerie, to the house Jim had built, and taken up the Quichua work that he had left. She did not see this as a heroic gesture. As she explained it, the work was there, the people were there, the language was one she could speak, and there was no one else to do it. The small church at Shandia, the schoolboys who had become young believers, the families in the surrounding settlements, all still needed teaching. It seemed to her simply the obvious next thing.

That phrase was to become her watchword. Years later she would often quote an anonymous old poem, its spelling as quaint as its date, whose refrain was “Doe the nexte thynge.” It counselled a troubled soul not to look too far ahead, but to take up the duty immediately in front of it and to leave the rest to God. Her return to Shandia was the thing it described. She did not have to solve the meaning of Jim’s death before going back to work. She had only to do what was in front of her.

The other widows made their own choices, and Elisabeth never suggested that hers was the only faithful one. Olive Fleming, who had been married less than two years and had no children, returned to the United States. Marilou McCully, who was expecting her third child, went home to the United States for the birth, and later returned to work in Quito. Marj Saint moved to Quito and stayed in Ecuador for some years. Barbara Youderian remained for a time among the Shuar in the south-east, carrying on the work she and Roger had shared. Each of them had to rebuild a life, and each did it differently.

A House With a Gap in It

Life at Shandia without Jim was harder than anything Elisabeth had known. She now carried the whole of the station’s work: the teaching, the medical care, the language, the correspondence, the household and a baby. She had the help of the Quichua believers, some of whom took on more responsibility in the church, and of colleagues on the other stations. Nate’s replacement pilots kept the supplies coming. But the house had a gap in it, and the evenings were long. Valerie gave her both a reason to keep going and a daily reminder of what had been lost. The child learned to walk and to talk in the house her father had built, watched over by a mother who now had to be everything to her, and surrounded by Quichua neighbours for whom a fatherless child was nothing unusual.

She also had something new to deal with. The story of the five men had gone round the world, and letters began to arrive at Shandia in great numbers from strangers who had been moved by it. Many of them wrote to say that they had given their lives to God, or to missionary work, because of what they had read. Others asked questions she could not answer. She replied to as many as she could. And she was asked, almost at once, to write the story herself.

The verse at the head of this chapter is from Psalm 68. God, says the psalmist, is a father to the fatherless and a judge, a defender, of widows. It is a promise she clung to in those months, and she would later say, often and plainly, that she had found it true. She was never sentimental about widowhood. She knew it was a loss and not a calling, and she would know it twice. But she found that God kept his word, not by removing the loss, but by being present in it, day after day, at Shandia, while she did the next thing.

fields.title: Through Gates of Splendor
fields.body_html:
“By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.”

— Hebrews 11:4, KJV

Asked to Write

Within weeks of the deaths on the Curaray, the story of the five men had been told to millions. Life magazine’s photo essay, built around Cornell Capa’s pictures of the widows and the search and around photographs the men had taken themselves on the beach, appeared at the end of January 1956. Newspapers, magazines and radio programmes followed. Churches across the United States held memorial services. Many accounts were hurried, and some were inaccurate. It was soon clear that someone who had known the men, and who could write, should tell the story properly. The obvious person was Elisabeth.

She agreed, and she worked quickly. She had at her disposal the men’s own diaries and letters, the notes Nate Saint had kept on the gift flights, the photographs, the recollections of the other widows and of the colleagues who had flown and searched, and her own memory. The book was written in the course of 1956, and it was published in 1957 by Harper and Brothers in New York under the title Through Gates of Splendor.

The cost of that work is easy to pass over. To write the book she had to read, in the first months of her widowhood, page after page of her husband’s private journals and letters, and to reconstruct hour by hour the weeks that had ended in his death. She had to weigh what to include about four other families, each with its own grief, and to write about men she had known well without either flattering them or exposing them. She did it while still carrying the ordinary load of a mother and a missionary.

The title came from a hymn. Before the men left for the Curaray they had sung together “We Rest on Thee”, a hymn by Edith Gilling Cherry, a young Englishwoman who had died in 1897, set to the tune of Sibelius’s Finlandia. Its last verse looks forward to the day when believers, passing through the gates of pearly splendour, rest with Christ for ever. Elisabeth took her title from that line. It placed the deaths of the five men where they themselves would have placed them, in the hope of the resurrection.

The Book

Readers who come to Through Gates of Splendor today, expecting a pious tribute, are often surprised by it. It is a plain, factual, carefully restrained book. Elisabeth told the story chronologically, from the five men’s backgrounds and callings to their deaths and the search, and she let their own words, from their journals and letters, carry much of the weight. She described the gift flights and the days on the beach in detail, and she did not linger on the horror of the end. She did not preach. She did not claim to know why God had allowed it, and she did not claim that the story was finished. The book ends not with an explanation but with the conviction that God was sovereign over what had happened, and with the work still to be done.

fields.body_html:
“And I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not; I will lead them in paths that they have not known: I will make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight. These things will I do unto them, and not forsake them.”

— Isaiah 42:16, KJV

Dayuma

The way back to the Waorani, when it opened, did not come through any plan of the missionaries. It came through three Waorani women.

The first of them was Dayuma. She had grown up among her people at a time of especially savage feuding, and some years before the events at Palm Beach, after members of her family had been killed, she had fled the forest. She found refuge among the Quichua and eventually came to work, in conditions close to servitude, on a hacienda in the foothills owned by a landowner named Carlos Sevilla. There she learned Quichua and some Spanish, and lived a life cut off from her own people, whom she believed she could never safely rejoin. It was there that Jim had gone to learn his handful of Waorani phrases from her, and there that Rachel Saint, Nate’s sister, a missionary with the Wycliffe Bible Translators and their Summer Institute of Linguistics, had been living for some time, learning the Waorani language from her.

After the deaths of the five men, Rachel’s work with Dayuma took on a new importance in the eyes of evangelicals at home. In 1957 Rachel took Dayuma to the United States. There the two women appeared before very large audiences, including the American television programme This Is Your Life and Billy Graham’s crusade at Madison Square Garden in New York. During these months Dayuma professed faith in Christ. For many American Christians she became the living sign that the story of Palm Beach would have a happy ending. The attention was intense, and some who knew both women later wondered whether it had been good for either of them.

Two Women on the Curaray

Elisabeth was not part of any of this. In November 1957 she was at Arajuno, the station on the edge of Waorani country that had been Ed McCully’s, when two Quichua men came in from the Curaray with startling news. Two Waorani women had come out of the forest and were at their house. Elisabeth went at once.

The women were Mankamu and Mintaka. They were older women, by most accounts kin of Dayuma, and they had walked out of their own territory into the Quichua country for reasons of their own, which outsiders never fully understood. Some accounts say they hoped to find out what had become of Dayuma, and that the feuding and grief among their own people had made them willing to risk the world outside. Mintaka was the older woman who had visited the five missionaries on the sandbar on 6 January 1956, less than two years before. She had seen them alive on the last Friday of their lives.

Elisabeth took the two women back with her to Shandia, and for the next ten months they lived with her and Valerie there. It was an extraordinary arrangement, and it was entered into without fuss. She gave them food and shelter and whatever care they needed, and they gave her, without quite intending to, what she most needed if she was ever to reach their people: the language. Day after day she listened to them, wrote down what she heard, and tried to make sense of it.

A Language Like No Other

It was the hardest linguistic task of her life. The Waorani language is unrelated to any other known language. It has nothing in common with Quichua or Spanish, and none of the ordinary aids to learning existed: no grammar, no dictionary, no other speaker to compare notes with except Rachel and Dayuma, who were far away in the United States. Elisabeth had to work out its sounds, its words and its structure from scratch, from two women who had never been asked to explain their language to anyone and who could not read or write. She did so with the methods she had learned at the Summer Institute of Linguistics and practised among the Colorados. Progress was slow, and every misunderstanding was a reminder of how little she knew.

The two women were not specimens or informants to her, nor were they simply converts in waiting. She came to know them as people, with their own humour, sorrows and opinions, and with their own way of seeing the strange world into which they had come. Her later writing about the Waorani is notable for its refusal either to romanticise them as noble innocents or to describe them as monsters. She had learned that refusal, in part, from living with Mintaka and Mankamu at Shandia.

The Three Go Home

In 1958 Rachel Saint and Dayuma returned to Ecuador. Dayuma met the two women from her own people, the first she had seen in more than ten years, and the three of them began to talk of going home together. On 3 September 1958, by the date usually given, Dayuma, Mintaka and Mankamu walked into the forest. Those left behind did not know whether they would see them again, or what reception the women would meet.

They came back about three weeks later, to Arajuno, where Elisabeth was waiting for them. With them came a party of Waorani, men and women, accounts differ on the number. They brought news that Dayuma’s people were alive, that they had heard what the three women had to say about the foreigners outside, and that they were willing to receive visitors. More than that, they brought an invitation. Elisabeth and Rachel were asked to come and live among them.

It was the moment that Jim and his friends had prayed for, and it had come in a way none of them could have planned. Not a plane and a loudspeaker, but a widow who had taken two women into her home, and an exile who had come back with news of her own. Elisabeth did not pretend, then or later, that she understood fully what God was doing. But she could see that a door had opened, and she had spent her life believing that when God opened a door the right response was to walk through it.

The verse at the head of this chapter is from Isaiah. God promises to lead the blind by a way they do not know, along paths they have not travelled, and to make crooked things straight. None of the people in this chapter could see far ahead: not the two Waorani women who walked out of the forest, not the exile on the hacienda, not the widow at Shandia. But the paths converged. In October 1958 Elisabeth Elliot, with her three-year-old daughter, set out to live among the people who had killed her husband.

fields.title: Into the Forest
fields.body_html:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”

— Romans 12:21, KJV

A Reckless Decision?

Not everyone thought Elisabeth should go. To many of her friends and relatives at home, the idea of a young widow taking a three-year-old child to live among the people who had speared her husband, less than three years before, seemed reckless to the point of folly. The Waorani had killed outsiders for generations. They had killed one another more often still. No one could guarantee that the invitation brought by the three women was meant by everyone in the group, or that it would be honoured if something went wrong. If Elisabeth were killed, Valerie would be an orphan. If Valerie were killed, it was hard to imagine what anyone would say.

Elisabeth weighed all this. She did not dismiss the danger, and she did not claim any special assurance that she would be kept safe. Her reasoning, as she later set it out, was simpler. The Waorani had asked her to come. She was one of the very few outsiders who had begun to learn their language. She believed that God had called her to make Christ known to people who had never heard of him, and these were such people. The risks were real, but they were not greater than the risks Jim had accepted, and she did not think that being a mother released her from obedience. She also did not think that obedience guaranteed a good outcome. She went anyway.

Those who have praised her for this decision have sometimes made it sound like an act of dramatic forgiveness, a widow going in search of her husband’s killers in order to love them. She did not describe it that way. She did not go as a widow on a mission of reconciliation. She went as a missionary to a people, and the fact that some of that people had killed Jim was, in her own telling, part of the situation rather than the point of it. Forgiveness was real and necessary, but it was not a performance. It was simply the condition of going at all.

The Clearing

Early in October 1958 Elisabeth, Valerie and Rachel Saint set out from the edge of the Quichua country with Dayuma and the Waorani who had come out to fetch them. The journey was made on foot through the forest. It was hard going for the adults and harder for a small child, who had to be carried. On 8 October 1958, by the date usually given, they reached the Waorani clearing beside a small river called the Tiwaeno, from which the settlement took its name. It was, as it happened, the day Jim would have turned thirty-one, and the fifth anniversary of their wedding.

The houses were large shelters thatched with palm leaves, with hammocks slung inside. The people grew manioc and plantains in clearings cut from the forest, hunted monkeys and birds with blowguns and spears, and fished in the rivers. They wore almost nothing. Most of them had never seen a foreigner close at hand, let alone a fair-haired child.

Elisabeth and Valerie lived as the Waorani did, in a simple thatched shelter, and Rachel lived close by. The Waorani gave Elisabeth a name: Gikari, which means woodpecker. Valerie began to pick up Waorani from the children she played with.

The bridge between the two worlds was Dayuma. She was home among her own kin after more than a decade away, and she was the only person in the clearing who could move easily between the Waorani and the foreigners. She began, in her own way, to tell her people the Bible stories she had learned, using for God the name Waengongi, the creator of Waorani tradition. Neither Elisabeth nor Rachel could yet speak well enough to do the same. In those first months the two outsiders depended on Dayuma for translation, for explanation of what they saw, and to a large degree for their own safety.

The Men

Among the people of the clearing were men who had been on the beach on 8 January 1956. Elisabeth met them in the first days. Gikita, the older man who had led the attack, was there. So were Kimo and Dyuwi, younger men, and Mincaye, who in later years would become the best known of them to the outside world through his friendship with Nate Saint’s son Steve. Nampa, Dayuma’s brother, had died since. Most of the men who had killed Jim were living within a few yards of his widow and his daughter.

What she felt on meeting them she later described with characteristic restraint. She did not claim to have felt nothing, and she did not claim to have felt only love. What struck her, again and again, was how ordinary they were. They were not monsters. They laughed, joked, quarrelled, cared for their children, mourned their dead, and went hunting. They had killed the five men, as they had killed many others, out of fear and anger and a long habit of violence, and in time they spoke of it plainly, as a thing that had happened. They had believed the foreigners were dangerous. They had been told that the foreigners had attacked their own people. In their world, killing those who threatened you was simply what one did.

She did not excuse what they had done. She did not pretend that it did not matter. But she also did not hate them. She had settled that question before she came. Now she had to live with it, day after day, at close quarters, in their houses and at their fires, while she tried to learn to speak to them.

Overcoming Evil

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s command at the end of the twelfth chapter of Romans: be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good. It is one of the hardest commands in the New Testament. Elisabeth did not claim to have kept it perfectly, and she would have been impatient with anyone who made her into a symbol of it. But the facts are plain. In October 1958 she went to live, with her child, among men who had killed her husband. She did not go to accuse them, to demand an apology, or to extract a dramatic scene of repentance for the benefit of supporters at home. She went to live with them, to learn their language, to give them what medical help she could, and to tell them about God.

Whether that would bear fruit, no one knew. What happened over the next three years was neither as quick nor as simple as the legend later claimed, and the next chapter tries to tell it honestly. But the first fact is the one worth pausing on. She went in. She took the child. She stayed.

But the facts are plain. In October 1958 she went to live, with her child, among men who had killed her husband. She did not go to accuse them, to demand an apology, or to extract a dramatic scene of repentance for the benefit of supporters at home. She went to live with them, to learn their language, to give them what medical help she could, and to tell them about God. Whether that would bear fruit, no one knew. What happened over the next three years was neither as quick nor as simple as the legend later claimed, and the next chapter tries to tell it honestly. But the first fact is the one worth pausing on. She went in. She took the child. She stayed.

fields.body_html:
“But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.”

— 2 Corinthians 4:7, KJV

Three Years at Tiwaeno

Elisabeth lived among the Waorani for about three years, from October 1958 until late in 1961. They were among the most demanding years of her life, and among the most important. For most of that time she was at Tiwaeno, sharing the life of the clearing: its food, its weather, its illnesses and its quarrels. She gave medicine to the sick, took photographs, kept notebooks and above all worked at the language. Valerie grew from a toddler into a little girl who ran barefoot with the Waorani children and spoke their language easily.

The language remained the central task. Elisabeth set out to analyse it as she had been trained to do, working out its sounds and grammar systematically and recording what she heard. It was slow, painstaking work, and she knew that any translation of Scripture worth the name would depend on getting it right. Dayuma, meanwhile, went on telling her people what she had learned of God in her own words. Rachel worked closely with Dayuma, and over time the Bible stories that Dayuma told, and the phrases that Rachel and Dayuma worked out together, became the main channel through which the Waorani heard the Christian message.

Something did begin to change. Over the years that followed, several of the people at Tiwaeno, including some of the men who had been on the beach in 1956, came to call themselves followers of God. Dayuma’s influence was crucial. Gikita, the old leader of the attack, and Kimo, Dyuwi and Mincaye were among those who in time professed faith, and some became leaders among the believers. The cycle of revenge spearing that had dominated Waorani life for generations began to slow among those who had settled around the missionaries, though it did not stop all at once, and other Waorani groups who had no contact with the missionaries went on killing and being killed for years. A few years after Elisabeth had left, Kimo and Dyuwi baptised two of Nate Saint’s children, Steve and Kathy, in the Curaray river, near the beach where their father had died.

The Savage My Kinsman

In 1961 Elisabeth published a book of photographs, with a spare accompanying text, about her first year among the Waorani. She called it The Savage My Kinsman. The title was itself a statement. Readers who had absorbed the language of savages and martyrs from the newspapers were confronted with pictures of men, women and children going about their lives, and with a title that insisted they were kin. The text did not claim mass conversions or a finished work. It showed a people, and a missionary among them, at the beginning of a long road.

The book was a sign of something else that was happening in her. Living with the Waorani, she had come to see how much of what she had brought with her was American culture rather than the gospel, and how little she could be sure of about what the people around her actually understood. She did not lose her faith. But she was becoming less certain of many things that the missionary movement at home took for granted, and more aware of how easily missionaries confused their own hopes with God’s work. Those questions would come out more fully in the years after she left Ecuador.

Two Strong Women

The hardest part of Tiwaeno was not the forest or the Waorani. It was Elisabeth’s relationship with Rachel Saint. The two women had come in together, and they shared the same faith and the same desire that the Waorani should know Christ. Each had lost someone on the beach: Rachel her brother, Elisabeth her husband. But they were very different people, and the differences proved impossible to bridge.

Historians who have studied the mission, especially Kathryn Long in God in the Rainforest (2019), describe differences of personality, of theology, of missionary method and of linguistic training. Rachel was older, intensely devoted, and convinced that God had given her a particular calling to the Waorani through Dayuma. She came to treat the work, and to some extent the people, as hers, and she was reluctant to share it with others or to cooperate with other missionaries and organisations. She relied heavily on Dayuma, and she saw the Waorani in the traditional evangelical terms of a people lost in darkness and waiting for the light. Elisabeth, the more highly trained linguist, wanted to work from a careful analysis of the language, and she was increasingly troubled by questions about how much the Waorani could understand of a message delivered largely through a single intermediary in a few years. The two could not agree on how to go about translation, which was meant to be the centre of their work.

Neither woman comes out of the story as simply right. Rachel’s possessiveness made life hard for Elisabeth and, later, for others. But Elisabeth could be cool, critical and quick to see the weaknesses in other people’s thinking, and she was not easy to work with either. Both were under enormous pressure, isolated, often unwell, and watched by an evangelical public that expected a triumphant story. Both were, in Paul’s phrase, earthen vessels. The friction between them is a reminder that God’s work among the Waorani was carried by fallible people, as all his work is.

Leaving

In late 1961 Elisabeth left Tiwaeno. Her reasons were several. The conflict with Rachel had made shared work almost impossible, and it was clear that Rachel, with Dayuma, was going to remain. Valerie was approaching school age. Elisabeth may also have come to believe that the Waorani work did not need two outsiders pulling in different directions. Whatever the balance of reasons, she went without public complaint. Rachel stayed, and she lived among the Waorani for most of the rest of her life.

Elisabeth went back to the Quichua work she had known before, and for about two more years she continued among the Quichua with Valerie. In 1963, when Valerie was eight, the two of them left Ecuador and returned to the United States, settling in Franconia, New Hampshire, where her family had spent so many summers. She had come to Ecuador in 1952 as a single woman of twenty-five. She left eleven years later, aged thirty-six, a widow with a daughter, the author of three books, and a far more questioning and far more seasoned Christian than the young linguist who had arrived.

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s description of the gospel and of those who carry it: a treasure in earthen vessels, so that the power may be seen to be God’s and not ours. Elisabeth’s Ecuador years had been full of loss, failure, misunderstanding and hard-won fruit, and almost none of it had gone the way anyone would have planned. She did not leave with a success story. She left with the conviction, which would shape everything she later wrote, that God does his work through cracked pots, and that he does not need the story to be tidy.

fields.title: The Questions She Would Not Hide
fields.body_html:
“Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.”

— Psalm 62:8, KJV

Franconia

In 1963 Elisabeth Elliot came home. She was thirty-six. She had spent eleven years in Ecuador: first among the Colorados of the western forest, then among the Quichua of the eastern jungle, and for three years among the Waorani on the Curaray. She brought back with her Valerie, then eight, who had spent a good part of her early childhood in a Waorani clearing and now had to learn how to be an American schoolgirl. The two of them settled in Franconia, New Hampshire, in the White Mountains, the place where the Howard family had spent its summers and where Elisabeth had known, since she was a child, the woods, the granite and the long, hard winters.

She was by then famous in a way that very few missionaries had ever been. Through Gates of Splendor and Shadow of the Almighty had sold in great numbers. Her photograph had appeared in Life. Churches, colleges and conferences across the country wanted the widow of Jim Elliot to come and tell them the story of Palm Beach. She had a child to support, and her living now came largely from writing and speaking, so she accepted a good many of the invitations. But the woman who stood up to speak was no longer quite the woman her audiences expected, and over the next few years that became increasingly plain.

What Ecuador Had Taught Her

The story of January 1956 had been told, in her own first book and in countless sermons since, as a story with a clear shape. Five young men had laid down their lives, and God had used their deaths to open a closed people to the gospel. Elisabeth never denied that God had been at work. She had seen it with her own eyes. Men who had speared her husband had become her neighbours, and some of them had become believers. But she had also seen, at very close range, how much of what happened did not fit the shape.

In San Miguel her language helper had been murdered and her work had been stolen. At Shandia she had lived on a station that the river had already once swept away. Among the Waorani the work had brought misunderstanding and rivalry among the missionaries as well as faith among the Indians, and her own time there had ended in strain with Rachel Saint. She had come away with hard questions about whether the missionaries, herself included, really understood what they were doing to a people’s whole way of life, and about how much of what they called the Lord’s work was in fact their own plans dressed up in pious language. Nothing in the sequence of her years in Ecuador had followed the logic of sacrifice and reward that devotional storytelling seemed to promise.

She came to believe that the honest thing was to say so. That conviction is the thread running through her writing in the 1960s. It made a good many of her readers uneasy, and it is a large part of the reason she is still read.

No Graven Image

In 1966 she published a novel, No Graven Image. Its heroine is a young, single missionary who goes to the highlands of Ecuador to reduce an unwritten Indian language to writing, in circumstances not unlike Elisabeth’s own at San Miguel. She longs for a faithful language helper and for the kind of fruit she has been taught to expect. Near the end of the book, trying to help, she gives an injection to the very man on whom her work depends, and he dies. The novel does not turn this into a lesson. It ends with the missionary stripped of her assumptions about what God must do, and with the unsettling suggestion that the God she had been serving was, at least in part, an image of her own making.

Many evangelical readers were dismayed. They had come to the author of Through Gates of Splendor for another story of triumph, and they found instead a missionary whose labours end in a death that serves no visible purpose. Some concluded that she had lost her faith, or was close to losing it. Others, then and since, have seen the novel as the most searching thing she ever wrote: not an attack on God, but on the idols that well-meaning Christians set up in his place. The title comes from the second commandment. The book was her way of saying that a God who must always produce the results we have planned for him is not the God of the Bible, but a carved image with a Christian name.

Two more books followed in 1968. Who Shall Ascend was a life of R. Kenneth Strachan, the general director of the Latin America Mission, who had died a few years before. She had been asked to write it, and she wrote it in the way she now believed a missionary life ought to be written, leaving in his doubts, his inner conflicts and his sense of failure rather than polishing them away. Some of those who had hoped for a tribute were disappointed. Others recognised in it a rare and humane honesty about the cost of Christian leadership.

The Liberty of Obedience, a short book, set out a theme that would run through the rest of her life. Christian freedom, she argued, is not found by escaping obedience to God but inside it. In the same book she questioned some of the rules and taboos by which evangelicals of her generation tended to measure holiness, and asked whether they had become a substitute for the harder obedience of the heart. The book was both a defence of submission to God and a protest against submission to mere convention, and readers on both sides found things in it they did not like.

Pouring Out the Heart

It would be easy to read these years as a crisis of faith, and some did at the time. The sources do not support so simple a picture. Her letters and journals from the period, on which her authorised biographer has drawn, show a woman who was lonely, often unsure of what she should do next, and doubtful about much that passed for missionary strategy. They do not show a woman abandoning Christ. What she abandoned was the habit of tidying things up. She came to think that the Christian’s business is to trust God, not to explain him, and that the faithful thing to do with an unanswered question is to bring it to him rather than to hide it, whether from him or from other people.

Her honesty was not always gentle. She could be blunt to the point of severity, she had little patience with sentiment, and some who met her in these years found her cool and hard to know. Part of that was temperament. Part of it, perhaps, was the armour of a woman who had been widowed young, who had been made into a public symbol of a story she knew was more complicated than its admirers wanted, and who had decided that she would not pretend.

That is what the psalm at the head of this chapter commends. The psalmist does not tell the people to compose themselves before they come to God, or to present him with a cleaned-up account of their lives. He tells them to pour out their hearts before him, because God is a refuge, and a refuge is a place for people who are in trouble. Elisabeth Elliot’s refusal to hide her questions cost her some admirers in the 1960s. It also prepared her, in ways she could not yet see, to speak in later years to the bereaved, the lonely and the bewildered with an authority that no tidy story could have given her.

fields.title: Addison Leitch
fields.body_html:
“Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.”

— Ecclesiastes 4:9, KJV

A Theologian from Pittsburgh

Addison Hardie Leitch was born in 1908 in Ben Avon, Pennsylvania, a small town on the Ohio River just below Pittsburgh, and he grew up in that part of the state. As a young man he went out to Egypt under the foreign mission board of the United Presbyterian Church of North America and taught science for a year or so at Assiut College, on the Nile. He came home to study for the ministry at Pittsburgh-Xenia Theological Seminary, and in 1936 he married Margaret Heslip. He then went on to Cambridge, where he took a doctorate in 1938. He and Margaret had four daughters.

His career was spent in the colleges and seminaries of American Presbyterianism. In the early 1940s he was dean of men and college pastor at Grove City College in western Pennsylvania. From 1946 he taught at his old seminary in Pittsburgh, and for some years in the later 1950s he was its president. In 1961 he moved to Tarkio College, a small Presbyterian college in north-western Missouri, as professor of philosophy and religion. He was also a well-known writer for the evangelical press and a regular contributor to Christianity Today. Those who knew him remembered a big personality: a lively, funny, well-read man, a gifted teacher, at ease in argument and at home in the pulpit.

A Second Marriage

He and Elisabeth Elliot met in the later 1960s; most accounts connect their meeting with one of her speaking engagements, and some date it to 1967. By the accounts of those who knew them, she was quickly drawn to him. Here, for the first time since 1956, was a man who was her equal in mind and in conviction, who had read what she had read, and who was not overawed by her fame. Margaret Leitch was by then seriously ill, and she died in 1968. The friendship between Addison and Elisabeth moved quickly after Margaret’s death, and before the year was out they were engaged. The speed of it surprised some of their friends and troubled a few. The sources do not suggest anything improper, and this book does not speculate beyond them; it records only that both of them had known long loneliness and that neither saw any reason to wait.

They were married on New Year’s Day, 1 January 1969. Elisabeth was forty-two; Addison was sixty. She had been a widow for thirteen years.

The marriage brought her east again, though not back to New Hampshire. That same year Addison joined the faculty of the newly formed Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary, in Hamilton, on the North Shore of Massachusetts, to teach theology. Elisabeth left Franconia, and she and Valerie, now a teenager, moved with him to Hamilton. The North Shore was to be her home for the rest of her life.

The seminary itself was new. It had been formed in 1969 by the merger of Gordon Divinity School, in Wenham, and the Conwell School of Theology, in Philadelphia, with the encouragement of Billy Graham and the support of a number of evangelical leaders and benefactors, and its first president was Harold John Ockenga. Its campus, on a wooded hill in Hamilton, had previously belonged to a Roman Catholic religious order. Addison came to it as a senior and experienced teacher, and he was one of the scholars who gave the young school its early standing. For Valerie the marriage meant a new home, a new school, a stepfather and four stepsisters, all of them a good deal older than she was. She had spent her childhood with one parent; now she had two.

Four Good Years

By the accounts of those who knew them, the years with Addison were happy ones. He was, by these accounts, warm and protective, and he enjoyed her company and her mind. She, who had been both mother and father to Valerie for most of the girl’s life, now had a husband to share the burden and a household that was not organised around one woman’s capacity to cope. She went on writing and speaking, and he encouraged her to do both.

For a woman who would later teach a great deal about marriage, these years matter. Her first marriage had lasted little more than two years and had been lived almost entirely on a mission station, in two languages not her own, under the shadow of a dangerous plan. fields.title: Lars, and Magnolia
fields.body_html:
“God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land.”

— Psalm 68:6, KJV

A Widow in Hamilton

After Addison’s death Elisabeth stayed in Hamilton. She had a house, a church, friends at the seminary and a living to earn, and she went on earning it in the way she knew. She wrote, she spoke, and in 1974 she was appointed an adjunct professor at Gordon-Conwell, a post she held for about two years. Later, in 1981, she spent a year as writer-in-residence at Gordon College in nearby Wenham.

One of the lodgers in her house in those years was Lars Gren. He was ten years younger than Elisabeth, born in September 1936, and he had worked as a salesman before deciding, in middle life, to go to seminary and train as a hospital chaplain. Over the following years a friendship grew between them, and the friendship became something more. In December 1977, four years after Addison’s death, they were married. Elisabeth was turning fifty-one, and it was her third marriage. She went on writing and speaking as Elisabeth Elliot, the name under which her readers knew her.

Let Me Be a Woman

In the same years Valerie grew up and married. Her husband, Walter Shepard, was to become a Presbyterian minister, and in time they had eight children, so that the woman who had once been a young widow with a single baby in the Ecuadorian jungle became the grandmother of a large family. Around the time of Valerie’s marriage Elisabeth wrote her a series of letters about what it meant to be a woman, a wife and a Christian. They were published in 1976 as Let Me Be a Woman. In 1981 she followed it with The Mark of a Man, a companion book addressed to men.

These books, and the many talks she gave on the same themes in the decades that followed, made her one of the best-known evangelical voices on men and women. She taught that the difference between the sexes is a gift of God and not an accident of culture, that a Christian woman should receive her womanhood gladly rather than resent it, and that in marriage a wife is called to submit to her husband’s headship as the church submits to Christ. Admirers and critics alike noticed that she herself had done things few women of her generation had done: she had gone alone to the forest, reduced an unwritten language to writing and lived among a people whom most outsiders feared. She saw no contradiction. In her view a single woman was free to serve God in ways a wife might not be, and submission in marriage was a particular calling within a particular relationship, not a judgement on the worth or abilities of women in general. She wrote against the feminist movement of the 1970s as she understood it, and she believed it had taught women to despise the very callings in which many of them could most fully serve God.

Many readers found in her teaching a clarity and a dignity they had looked for in vain elsewhere. Women who were wives and mothers, often quietly and without recognition, heard from her that their work was a calling and not a consolation prize. Others, including many evangelicals who believed that Scripture teaches the full equality of men and women in the home and the church, criticised her sharply. They argued that she read the Bible through the conventions of mid-century American life, that her own career as a pioneer missionary, linguist, author and public speaker sat awkwardly with what she told other women, and that teaching on submission given without enough qualification could be used to keep women in marriages that were harming them. The debate continues among Christians who love the Bible on both sides of it. This book is the story of her life, not an assessment of her teaching; the companion volume, The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot, weighs her views under Scripture. It is enough to say here that she held them sincerely, that she believed she was obeying God in teaching them, and that she did not retreat from them when she was criticised.

Magnolia

In time Elisabeth and Lars made their home in Magnolia, a village on the rocky coast of Cape Ann, part of the city of Gloucester, a few miles from Hamilton. The house stood close to the sea. It was from there that she wrote most of her later books and went out to most of her later engagements.

Lars took charge of the business side of her ministry. He managed her diary, made the arrangements for her travels, handled much of her publishing and oversaw the sale of her books, and for many years he travelled with her almost everywhere she went. Her public work grew enormously during their marriage, and it is unlikely that it would have taken the shape it did without his energy and organisation.

A Harder Marriage Than It Looked

The marriage was, however, harder than most of her readers knew. The fullest account of it is in Ellen Vaughn’s authorised biography, whose second volume, Being Elisabeth Elliot, appeared in 2023, and what follows rests on that published account. Vaughn had much less to go on for these years than for the earlier ones, because, as she reports, Lars destroyed most of Elisabeth’s journals from the years of their marriage, a decision she says he came to regret. Drawing on the memories of family and close friends, Vaughn describes a husband given to outbursts of temper, who in time came to control much of Elisabeth’s daily life, including her diary and how often she saw her friends. Elisabeth herself did not speak of these things in public, and she remained married to him for the rest of her life.

A biography written for readers who loved her has to be honest here, as she would have wanted it to be, and it also has to be fair. This account depends on a source written after her death, from the testimony of those close to her, and Lars’s own perspective is largely missing from it. This book does not go beyond what Vaughn reports, and it does not presume to judge a marriage from the outside. It is also true, as a later chapter will show, that when her mind failed it was Lars who insisted on caring for her at home, and who did so for many years. Both things belong to the record, and neither cancels the other.

The verse at the head of this chapter says that God sets the solitary in families. Elisabeth Elliot had been solitary for much of her adult life. In these years God gave her a son-in-law, a household of grandchildren and a third husband, and the family he gave her was, like most families, both a mercy and a cross.

fields.title: Gateway to Joy
fields.body_html:
“The LORD hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.”

— Jeremiah 31:3, KJV

A Newsletter and a Shelf of Books

The 1980s were the most productive decade of Elisabeth Elliot’s public life. In her mid-fifties, settled on the North Shore with Lars managing her affairs, she began to write and speak at a pace that would have exhausted a younger woman, and the audience she reached grew far beyond the readers who had first known her as a missionary widow.

Around 1982 she began to send out a short newsletter of her own to anyone who asked for it. The Elisabeth Elliot Newsletter was a plain, personal publication: a few pages of reflection on a passage of Scripture or a question from a reader, news of her family and her travels, and a list of where she would be speaking. It ran for more than twenty years, until 2003, and many of her later books were gathered, wholly or partly, from its pages.

The books themselves came steadily. Discipline: The Glad Surrender (1982) set out her conviction that the disciplines of body, mind, time and feeling are not burdens laid on the Christian but ways of offering the whole of life to God. Passion and Purity (1984) told, for the first time at length and in her own words, the story of her slow, restrained courtship with Jim Elliot, and used it to urge young Christians to entrust their longings for love and marriage to God. It became one of the most widely read of all her books, especially among young evangelicals in America, and it shaped the way a generation thought about romance. In later years it was also criticised, by some who had grown up in the purity movement of the 1990s, for setting a standard of restraint that some readers had turned into a source of anxiety and shame. That debate belongs to the companion volume on her teaching.

In 1987 came A Chance to Die, her life of Amy Carmichael. It was in some ways the repayment of a debt. Elisabeth had read Amy Carmichael’s books as a girl, and the Irish missionary who had given her life to rescuing children in South India, and who founded the Dohnavur Fellowship there, had been one of the formative influences on her own call. The biography is warm but not uncritical, and it is still one of the best ways into Amy Carmichael’s life. Two of Amy Carmichael’s own books, Things as They Are and If, are in the Ochorus library.

Lincoln, Nebraska

In 1988 Back to the Bible, the radio ministry based in Lincoln, Nebraska, invited her to present a new daily programme for women. It was to be short, about a quarter of an hour, and broadcast on Christian stations across the United States and beyond. She agreed, and the programme was called Gateway to Joy. She spoke in the same clear, level, unhurried voice that audiences already knew from her conference addresses.

Each programme began in the same way. She reminded her listeners that they were loved with an everlasting love, as the verse at the head of this chapter says, and that underneath were the everlasting arms, in the words of Moses’ blessing in Deuteronomy. Then she introduced herself as their friend and turned to the day’s subject. For thirteen years, from 1988 to 2001, those two sentences of Scripture went out to a very large audience, and for many listeners they became the thing they remembered best.

The subjects were often startlingly ordinary. She spoke about prayer and the will of God, about suffering and loneliness and widowhood, about marriage and the bringing up of children. But she also spoke about tidiness and punctuality, about manners and hospitality, about washing dishes and answering letters and getting up in the morning. Her conviction was that the Christian life is lived chiefly in such things, and that the faithful doing of small duties is not a lesser form of devotion than the dramatic sacrifices people admire. The programme was carried on Christian stations across America and, in time, in other countries too, and it reached women in kitchens and cars, in hospitals and nursing homes, at hours when few of them could have gone to a meeting. Listeners wrote to her and to Back to the Bible in great numbers, and many of them said that she had addressed them as adults, without flattery and without fuss.

On the Road

At the same time she spoke at conferences, churches, colleges and women’s meetings across America and in other countries, with Lars almost always beside her. The books continued. Loneliness (1988) drew on her widowhoods and on her single years in Ecuador. On Asking God Why (1989) was a collection of short essays on trust. A Path Through Suffering (1990) used the life of plants and the lessons of the countryside to think about pain and fruitfulness. Keep a Quiet Heart (1995) gathered pieces from the newsletter. Quest for Love (1996), a sequel to Passion and Purity, told the stories of other men and women who had tried to keep their love affairs under God’s rule.

Her manner did not soften with fame. She was crisp, direct and at times severe. She disliked sentimentality, self-pity and what she regarded as the cult of feelings in modern Christianity, and she said so. Some found her cold. Many more, especially women who were bereaved, lonely, unhappily single or simply worn out by ordinary duties, found her bracing. She did not tell them that their troubles were small. She told them that God was great and that he was with them in their troubles, and she spoke as one who had been through more than most of them.

Underneath

There is a certain irony in the shape of these years. The woman who opened every programme with the assurance of the everlasting arms was, as the previous chapter showed, carrying burdens at home that few of her listeners suspected, and, by Vaughn’s account, she was by temperament a reserved person for whom public life was often a strain. None of that appeared in the broadcasts. Some will see in that a failure of candour from a woman who prized candour. Others will see the discipline she taught: the refusal to make her own trials the subject of her ministry, and the resolve to point her hearers past herself.

Either way, the promise she repeated was not hers. It was God’s, spoken first through Jeremiah to a people in exile who had every reason to think he had stopped loving them. Elisabeth Elliot spent thirteen years telling ordinary people that it still held. There is good reason to think she was telling herself the same thing.

fields.title: The Next Thing
fields.body_html:
“Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.”

An Old Poem

The message was three words long: “Doe the nexte thynge.” The poem goes on to commend those words to anyone who is anxious, overwhelmed or uncertain of the way ahead. One need not see the whole road. On each occasion, the sources suggest, she did what lay in front of her: she cared for her child, she kept up her work, she answered her letters, she wrote the next page. The other conviction that ran through all her later work was that suffering, in the hands of God, is never wasted. She meant that God, who had brought the greatest good the world has known out of the cross of his Son, could be trusted to bring good out of the suffering of those who belong to him, even when they could not see how.

She came to that belief by the hard road. She had lost a language helper to murder and years of work to a thief. She had lost a husband to the spears of the very people she later went to live among, and another to cancer. She had seen the mission she had given herself to divided by quarrels. She did not claim to understand why any of these things had happened. What she claimed was that none of them had been for nothing, and she held to that claim to the end of her working life.

She was careful to distinguish this from a fatalist’s shrug. The Christian who suffers, in her teaching, is not simply giving in to what cannot be helped. He is trusting a Father who is known to be good, taking what comes as from his hand and giving it back to him. One of the next things she did, in the middle of her busiest years, was to go back to the story that had made her famous. In 1996, forty years after the deaths on Palm Beach, a new edition of Through Gates of Splendor was published with an epilogue in which she looked again at what had happened among the Waorani since 1956. She acknowledged that events had not unfolded as simply as the first edition, and the many sermons based on it, had suggested. Historians have since filled in that picture. Killings among the Waorani did not stop at once; the growth of the church among them was real but uneven; and the dealings between the outsiders and the Waorani, missionaries included, were more complicated, and in places more painful, than the early telling allowed.

It was not a recantation. She still believed that God had been at work in 1956 and afterwards, and that the five men had been right to go. But she would not let the story harden into a legend that served the comfort of its admirers at the expense of the truth. She had been saying the same thing, in one way or another, since the 1960s. Now she said it in the book itself.

That was a costly kind of honesty. Through Gates of Splendor was by then a classic of missionary literature, and many readers loved it exactly as it was. She did not need to disturb it. Her reputation would have been safer if she had left it alone. But she had learned at San Miguel, and in the writing of No Graven Image, that faith built on a story that is too good to be true is faith in the wrong thing.

Through these years her family grew. Valerie and Walter Shepard had eight children, and Elisabeth took a close interest in all of them. She had written The Shaping of a Christian Family in 1992, looking back on the home in which she had grown up, with its family worship, its hymns and its Scripture memory, and she hoped to see something of the same pattern carried on into the next generations.

She went on writing into her seventies. Collections of her shorter pieces, including Secure in the Everlasting Arms (2002) and Be Still My Soul (2003), gathered the work of many years. But by the turn of the century those around her had begun to notice changes. Gateway to Joy came to an end in 2001. The newsletter ended two years later. The next thing, for Elisabeth Elliot, was to be the hardest of all.
