He tells them to do with their might whatever their hand finds to do, because life is short and the opportunity will not last. She spent her life doing that, one duty at a time, and she believed that the God who gave the duties would take care of the rest.

fields.title: The Long Twilight
fields.body_html:
“And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you.”

— Isaiah 46:4, KJV

The Failing of Words

Elisabeth Elliot had lived by words. She had gone to Wheaton to study Greek so that she could translate the Scriptures. She had gone to Ecuador to reduce unwritten languages to writing, and she had worked in Spanish, in the Colorado language, in Quichua and in the language of the Waorani. She had written more than twenty books, thousands of pages of letters and newsletters, and the scripts of hundreds upon hundreds of radio talks, and she had spoken to audiences on several continents. Clarity of language was, for her, almost a moral matter. She disliked vagueness, jargon and sentiment because she thought they were ways of avoiding the truth.

It was her words that began to go first. In the late 1990s she and those closest to her began to notice lapses of memory and moments of confusion that could no longer be put down to tiredness or age, and by about 2000 she had been diagnosed with dementia; accounts differ by a year or two over the date. It progressed slowly at first. For a while she was able to continue some of her work, with help. Gateway to Joy ended in 2001, after thirteen years. The newsletter that had run for more than two decades ended in 2003, and in 2004 she gave up public speaking. After that she withdrew from public life altogether. The decision was made for her by the illness, but it was also, in its way, characteristic. She had always been a private person, and she did not become a spectacle in her decline. The public simply stopped hearing from her, and most of her readers learned only gradually, and at second hand, why.

There is a particular sorrow in the decline of a mind that has served God and others so well. Many who had been helped by her books felt it as a personal loss, and some wondered aloud how it could be that a woman who had taught so many people to trust God in suffering should herself be brought to a place where she could no longer speak of him. She had no answer to give them now. But she had given her answer long before. She had always insisted that God does not owe us an explanation, and that the suffering he permits is never for nothing, whether or not we are able to see its purpose. In her last years she was no longer able to say those things. She was left simply to live them.

At Home in Magnolia

Lars decided that she would stay at home. Rather than place her in a nursing home, he looked after her himself in the house at Magnolia for the rest of her life. It was a long and wearing task. Dementia lasted in her case for the better part of fifteen years, and in its later stages she needed care at every hour of the day. Whatever else is to be said about their marriage, and the previous chapters have tried to say it fairly, this was faithful service, and it deserves to be recorded. Lars was himself in his early sixties when the illness was diagnosed and nearly seventy-nine when it ended. Caring for someone with dementia at home is among the hardest kinds of love: unrelenting, largely unseen and usually unthanked by the very person for whom it is done, who often no longer knows who is caring for them. Families who have done it will recognise the cost.

Valerie and her family visited, and old friends came when they could. The illness took its usual slow course, and in time the woman whose words had reached millions could say very little. This book does not try to say more than that about her inward life in these years. No one can know it, and those who loved her have been rightly reticent about it.

15 June 2015

Elisabeth Elliot died at home in Magnolia on the morning of Monday 15 June 2015. She was eighty-eight. It was fifty-nine years since the deaths on the Curaray, nearly forty-two since the death of Addison Leitch, and more than a decade since she had last spoken in public.

Her funeral was held on Tuesday 23 June at the A. J. Gordon Memorial Chapel of Gordon College, in Wenham, not far from the places where she had spent the second half of her life. A month later, on 26 July, a memorial service was held at her old college, in the Edman Memorial Chapel at Wheaton, where she had studied Greek seventy years before. Tributes came from across the evangelical world and far beyond it, from people who had read her books in their youth, listened to her on the radio in their kitchens, or been sustained by her in times of grief. Many of them, inevitably, spoke of 1956, and of the young widow who had gone to live with the men who had killed her husband. That was the story the world remembered. Some of the more perceptive spoke instead of the long years afterwards, which had been, in their way, a harder test.

Lars Gren outlived her by nearly ten years. He died in Little Rock, Arkansas, on 2 April 2025, at the age of eighty-eight, and was buried in Hamilton, Massachusetts.

Carried

The verse at the head of this chapter was spoken by God through Isaiah to a people who had grown old under his care. He contrasts himself with the idols of Babylon, which have to be lifted onto the backs of beasts and carried. The true God does the opposite. He carries his people. He made them, he has borne them since they were born, and he will carry them even to their grey hairs.

Elisabeth Elliot had spent much of her life carrying others: a baby in the jungle, a grieving household, a dying husband, a public that wanted her to bear the weight of a story, and countless readers and listeners who brought their sorrows to her. In her last years she could carry nothing, not even her own memories. Someone else had to carry her, and, behind every human hand that did it, the One she had trusted since childhood carried her too. There is a lesson in that for a culture that measures the worth of a life by what a person can still do. For more than ten years Elisabeth Elliot could do almost nothing, and her life was no less precious to God, and no less a life of faith, than it had been when she stood before thousands. She had written for decades about the everlasting arms. In the long twilight of her life she had nothing left to rest on but those arms, and they held.

fields.title: The Legacy of Elisabeth Elliot
fields.body_html:
“Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.”

— Hebrews 13:7, KJV

The Books

When Elisabeth Elliot died in 2015 she had been silent for more than ten years, and some of her younger admirers knew her only as a name on the spine of a book their mothers had given them. Yet her books had never gone out of print. Through Gates of Splendor and Shadow of the Almighty were still being read as classics of missionary history, in English and in translation, and publishers have continued to issue new editions of her books in the years since her death. Passion and Purity, Let Me Be a Woman, Keep a Quiet Heart and A Chance to Die were still being given to young women, passed between friends and discussed in church study groups. In the years since her death, recordings of Gateway to Joy have been made available again, and a new generation has heard the old opening words about the everlasting love and the everlasting arms.

Her family has also opened the record of her early life. In 2019 Valerie Elliot Shepard published Devotedly, drawn from the letters and journals of her parents during their long courtship and short marriage. It allowed readers to hear Jim and Elisabeth in their own words, and it showed more fully than any earlier book how much the two of them had struggled, hoped and waited.

The Biographers

For most of her life the story of Elisabeth Elliot was told chiefly by Elisabeth Elliot. Since her death that has changed. Ellen Vaughn’s authorised biography, in two volumes, Becoming Elisabeth Elliot (2020) and Being Elisabeth Elliot (2023), was written with access to her surviving journals and letters through the co-operation of her family. It is warm and admiring, but it does not hide her faults or the difficulties of her marriages. Lucy S. R. Austen’s Elisabeth Elliot: A Life (2023) is an independent biography, the fruit of long work in the sources. And the historian Kathryn T. Long’s God in the Rainforest (2019) set the events of 1956 and after in the full history of the mission to the Waorani.

Many missionaries of the generations after hers have said that her books, and the story of Jim and his companions, were among the things that first turned their thoughts towards serving Christ overseas, and many others, who never left home, have said that she taught them how to grieve. These biographies have not diminished her. If anything they have made her more credible. The woman who emerges from them is more complicated than the saint of the evangelical imagination: proud at times, often lonely, sometimes harsh, prone to discouragement, and capable of serious misjudgements. She is also, unmistakably, a woman who kept faith with Christ through a long and costly life, and who never stopped trying to tell the truth about it.

The story that made her famous has also been retold. Long and other historians have shown how much of what happened among the Waorani after 1956 depended on the Waorani themselves: on Dayuma, who carried the message back to her own people; on Mintaka and Mankamu, who came out of the forest and went back into it; and on the decisions of Waorani men and women who chose to put down the spear. Missionaries, including Elisabeth and Rachel Saint, played their part, sometimes wisely and sometimes not. The life of the Waorani people in the decades since has included real Christian faith, painful change and continuing struggles over land and the oil industry, and their own voices are now heard in its telling. Some of the men who had taken part in the killings lived to old age as Christian leaders among their own people. One of them, Mincaye, became a close friend of Nate Saint’s son Steve and travelled with him in the United States, telling his own story to audiences who had grown up on the story of 1956, and the friendship was the subject of a feature film, End of the Spear, released in 2006.

Elisabeth would not have objected to this. In a sense she began it. Her epilogue of 1996, and the long refusal behind it to let the story of Palm Beach become a legend, prepared her readers for a fuller and more honest account than the one she had first written as a grieving widow not yet thirty.

Where She Must Be Weighed

Gratitude for her life is not the same as agreement with everything she taught. Her views on men and women, marriage and submission remain contested among Christians who take Scripture seriously, and the arguments on both sides deserve a hearing. Passion and Purity has been criticised by some who grew up in the purity movement it helped to shape. Her bluntness wounded some who came to her for help. The early, triumphant telling of 1956, in which she played a large part, encouraged a style of missionary storytelling that she herself later worked to correct. These questions belong chiefly to her teaching, and they are considered in the companion volume, The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot. They are named here so that no reader mistakes this book’s gratitude for an endorsement of everything she said. She would have wanted every claim tested by Scripture, and she would have been the first to point her readers past herself to Christ.

Considering the End

The verse at the head of this chapter tells Christians to remember those who have spoken to them the word of God, and to follow their faith, considering the end of their conversation, that is, the outcome of their whole manner of life. It does not tell us to copy them in everything. It tells us to look at how their lives turned out, and to follow the faith that carried them there.

Considered in that way, the life of Elisabeth Elliot is a remarkable witness. A girl from a strict and loving Philadelphia household learned Greek to translate the Bible, went alone to the forests of Ecuador, lost her work, her helper and her husband, went to live with the men who had killed him, came home with her questions unhidden, was widowed again, married a third time into a harder life than anyone saw, spoke to millions, and then, for her last ten years and more, was silent. Through all of it she held, sometimes grimly, to the conviction that God is sovereign, that he is good, and that nothing offered to him is ever wasted. The courage of 1956 made her famous. The courage of the long decades afterwards, the courage to obey, to tell the truth and to keep going, is the reason she is still worth following. One does not have to agree with everything she taught to see that, or to be grateful for it.

Long and other historians have shown how much of what happened among the Waorani after 1956 depended on the Waorani themselves: on Dayuma, who carried the message back to her own people; on Mintaka and Mankamu, who came out of the forest and went back into it; and on the decisions of Waorani men and women who chose to put down the spear. Missionaries, including Elisabeth and Rachel Saint, played their part, sometimes wisely and sometimes not. The life of the Waorani people in the decades since has included real Christian faith, painful change and continuing struggles over land and the oil industry, and their own voices are now heard in its telling. Some of the men who had taken part in the killings lived to old age as Christian leaders among their own people. One of them, Mincaye, became a close friend of Nate Saint’s son Steve and travelled with him in the United States, telling his own story to audiences who had grown up on the story of 1956, and the friendship was the subject of a feature film, End of the Spear, released in 2006. Elisabeth would not have objected to this. In a sense she began it. Her epilogue of 1996, and the long refusal behind it to let the story of Palm Beach become a legend, prepared her readers for a fuller and more honest account than the one she had first written as a grieving widow not yet thirty. Where She Must Be Weighed Gratitude for her life is not the same as agreement with everything she taught. Her views on men and women, marriage and submission remain contested among Christians who take Scripture seriously, and the arguments on both sides deserve a hearing. Passion and Purity has been criticised by some who grew up in the purity movement it helped to shape. Her bluntness wounded some who came to her for help. The early, triumphant telling of 1956, in which she played a large part, encouraged a style of missionary storytelling that she herself later worked to correct. These questions belong chiefly to her teaching, and they are considered in the companion volume, The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot. They are named here so that no reader mistakes this book’s gratitude for an endorsement of everything she said. She would have wanted every claim tested by Scripture, and she would have been the first to point her readers past herself to Christ. Considering the End The verse at the head of this chapter tells Christians to remember those who have spoken to them the word of God, and to follow their faith, considering the end of their conversation, that is, the outcome of their whole manner of life. It does not tell us to copy them in everything. It tells us to look at how their lives turned out, and to follow the faith that carried them there. Considered in that way, the life of Elisabeth Elliot is a remarkable witness. A girl from a strict and loving Philadelphia household learned Greek to translate the Bible, went alone to the forests of Ecuador, lost her work, her helper and her husband, went to live with the men who had killed him, came home with her questions unhidden, was widowed again, married a third time into a harder life than anyone saw, spoke to millions, and then, for her last ten years and more, was silent. Through all of it she held, sometimes grimly, to the conviction that God is sovereign, that he is good, and that nothing offered to him is ever wasted. The courage of 1956 made her famous. The courage of the long decades afterwards, the courage to obey, to tell the truth and to keep going, is the reason she is still worth following. One does not have to agree with everything she taught to see that, or to be grateful for it.

fields.title: Appendix A: Lessons from the Life of Elisabeth Elliot
fields.body_html:
“For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.”

— Romans 15:4, KJV

The lessons below are not a summary of Elisabeth Elliot’s teaching, which is set out in the companion volume. They are lessons drawn from her life, the things her story suggests to anyone trying to follow Christ. Each is set beside a passage of Scripture, because her life is worth learning from only in so far as it points back to the Word she trusted.

1. Obedience Comes Before Understanding

Again and again she had to act without knowing how things would turn out: going to Ecuador single, marrying a man who had made her wait for years, going into the forest with a small child. She did not wait for explanations before she obeyed. “Jesus answered and said unto him, What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter” (John 13:7, KJV).

2. Waiting Is Not Wasted

Her courtship with Jim Elliot lasted five years, most of them spent apart and in uncertainty. She learned to entrust her longings to God rather than to seize them. The waiting shaped her as much as the having did. “Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD” (Psalm 27:14, KJV).

3. Loss Can Be Offered to God

A murdered helper, a stolen suitcase of language work, a husband speared on a sandbar: she did not pretend these losses were small. She learned to offer them to God as she would have offered a gift, and to trust that nothing so offered is wasted. “And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28, KJV).

4. Love Your Enemies, Literally

Within three years of Jim’s death she was living among the men who had killed him, sharing their food and learning their language. Some of them became her brothers in Christ. Forgiveness for her was not a feeling but a place to live. “But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44, KJV).

5. Tell the Truth, Even About Heroes

She would not let the story of 1956 harden into a legend. She told the truth about missionary failures, including her own, and she added an epilogue to her most famous book to do it. Christians do not need flattering stories to sustain their faith. “Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another” (Ephesians 4:25, KJV).

6. God Is Not Our Tool

In No Graven Image she exposed the habit of treating God as a means to the results we want. She learned in Ecuador that he will not be managed, and that his purposes are larger than our plans. “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD” (Isaiah 55:8, KJV).

7. Questions Belong in Prayer

She did not hide her doubts, either from God or from her readers. She brought them to him. Honest lament is not the opposite of faith but one of its forms. “Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8, KJV).

8. Do the Next Thing

When the whole road was hidden, she did the duty in front of her. Her watchword, borrowed from an old poem, is a cure for the anxiety that tries to live tomorrow today. “Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof” (Matthew 6:34, KJV).

9. Small Duties Are Holy

For thirteen years she spoke on the radio about washing dishes, keeping promises and answering letters as well as about prayer and suffering. She believed that God is served in ordinary things as truly as in dramatic ones. “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10, KJV).

10. Grief Is Real, and So Is Hope

Widowed twice, she grieved in earnest, and she would not hurry others through their grief. But she grieved as one who believed in the resurrection. “But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13, KJV).

11. Saints Are Sinners Being Made Holy

Her biographers have shown her pride, her severity and the difficulties of her home life. None of that makes her less worth learning from. It shows that God works through flawed people, and that the faith we follow is finally Christ’s, not theirs. “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psalm 146:3, KJV).

12. God Carries Us to the End

In her last years she could neither teach nor write nor remember. She was carried, by her husband and by her God. Faithfulness in old age is sometimes simply a matter of being held. “Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come” (Psalm 71:18, KJV).

fields.title: Appendix B: Chapter-by-Chapter Study and Reflection Guide
fields.body_html:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.”

— James 1:22, KJV

This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a reading course of about twenty-four weeks. Its purpose is not to make Elisabeth Elliot an object of admiration, but to let her life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse and to end with prayer. Those who want to go further are encouraged to read her own books, obtained from their publishers or a library, alongside these chapters.

Chapter 1 - Brussels and Germantown

Central idea

Elisabeth Howard was born to missionary parents in Brussels and raised in a large, devout Philadelphia family, where her father edited the Sunday School Times.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 139:13-16; Psalm 16:6; Acts 17:26.

Reflection

1. What did the faith of your family, or its absence, give you? 2. Where has God placed you, and to what end?

Chapter 2 - A House Ordered by Scripture

Central idea

Family worship, hymns, Scripture memory, firm discipline and summers in Franconia formed habits of faith that lasted her whole life.

Scriptures to revisit

Deuteronomy 6:6-7; Joshua 24:15; 2 Timothy 3:14-15.

Reflection

1. What habits of faith shape your household? 2. Which passages of Scripture do you know by heart, and which would you like to?

Chapter 3 - Hampden DuBose

Central idea

At a Christian boarding school in Florida a shy, serious girl was stretched and tested, and her sense of a call to missionary service grew.

Scriptures to revisit

Ecclesiastes 12:1; 1 Samuel 3:10; Isaiah 6:8.

Reflection

1. When did you first sense that God might have work for you to do? 2. Who encouraged you then?

Chapter 4 - Greek at Wheaton

Central idea

She studied classical Greek so that she could translate the Scriptures, and she met Jim Elliot, her brother’s friend.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 2:3-5; 2 Timothy 2:15; Psalm 119:130.

Reflection

1. How are you using your mind in the service of God’s Word? 2. What friendships has God used to change the direction of your life?

Chapter 5 - A Love Laid on the Altar

Central idea

Elisabeth and Jim acknowledged their love but gave it back to God, uncertain whether he would ever allow them to marry.

Scriptures to revisit

Genesis 22:1-14; Romans 12:1; Psalm 37:4-5.

Reflection

1. What desire are you holding most tightly? 2. What would it mean to lay it on the altar?

Chapter 6 - The Waiting Years

Central idea

Years of separation, letters, study at Prairie Bible Institute and training in linguistics tested two young people’s patience and faith.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 27:14; Lamentations 3:25-26; Isaiah 40:31.

Reflection

1. What are you waiting for, and how are you waiting? 2. How has a season of waiting shaped you?

Chapter 7 - San Miguel de los Colorados

Central idea

As a single missionary in the western forest of Ecuador, she set out with other women to reduce the Colorado language to writing.

Scriptures to revisit

Romans 10:14-15; Psalm 96:3; Matthew 28:19-20.

Reflection

1. Who around you has never heard the gospel in words they understand? 2. What part might you play?

Chapter 8 - Macario, and a Stolen Suitcase

Central idea

Her language helper was murdered and her work was stolen: losses that no explanation could make sense of.

Scriptures to revisit

Job 1:21; Habakkuk 3:17-18; 2 Corinthians 4:8-9.

Reflection

1. What loss in your life has never been explained? 2. Can you offer it to God without an explanation?

Chapter 9 - Quichua First

Central idea

Engaged in January 1953, she set aside her own plans to learn Quichua in the eastern jungle before marrying Jim.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 16:9; Philippians 2:3-4; James 4:13-15.

Reflection

1. Whose plans govern your life? 2. What would yielding a plan cost you this year?

Chapter 10 - 8 October 1953

Central idea

A civil wedding in Quito on Jim’s twenty-sixth birthday began a marriage with very little ceremony and a great deal of purpose.

Scriptures to revisit

Genesis 2:24; Ecclesiastes 4:9-12; Ephesians 5:25.

Reflection

1. What makes a marriage strong when outward things are plain? 2. How can you honour the marriages around you?

Chapter 11 - Shandia

Central idea

Married life among the Quichua, on a station rebuilt after a flood, and the birth of Valerie in February 1955.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 127:3; 1 Corinthians 15:58; Galatians 6:9.

Reflection

1. Where is your labour unseen? 2. How do you keep going when the fruit is slow?

Chapter 12 - Palm Beach

Central idea

Five young men set out to reach the Waorani, agreed not to use their guns against them, and were killed on 8 January 1956.

Scriptures to revisit

John 12:24-25; John 15:13; Revelation 12:11.

Reflection

1. What would you refuse to do even to save your own life? 2. How do you weigh courage against prudence?

Chapter 13 - The Widow at Shandia

Central idea

Widowed at twenty-nine with a baby of ten months, she stayed in Ecuador and went on with the work.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 46:1-2; Isaiah 43:2; 2 Corinthians 1:3-4.

Reflection

1. How has God met you in grief? 2. Whom do you know who needs comfort now?

Chapter 14 - Through Gates of Splendor

Central idea

She told the story of the five men, and of Jim’s life, in books that reached millions and turned grief into a public witness.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 145:4; Habakkuk 2:2; Hebrews 11:4.

Reflection

1. What story of God’s work should you write down or tell? 2. How do we honour the dead without making legends of them?

Chapter 15 - Mintaka and Mankamu

Central idea

Two Waorani women came out of the forest and lived with her, while Dayuma taught her language to Rachel Saint.

Scriptures to revisit

Ruth 2:10-12; Hebrews 13:2; Romans 12:20-21.

Reflection

1. Who is the stranger at your door? 2. What would it cost you to welcome them?

Chapter 16 - Into the Forest

Central idea

In October 1958 she, Valerie and Rachel Saint went to live among the people who had killed her husband.

Scriptures to revisit

Genesis 12:1; Psalm 23:4; Matthew 5:44.

Reflection

1. Where is God asking you to go that you would rather not? 2. Whom do you need to forgive in practice, not only in word?

Chapter 17 - Among the Waorani

Central idea

Some of the killers became believers, but strain among the missionaries and her own questions led her to leave, and in 1963 to return home.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 5:17; Acts 15:36-40; Philippians 4:2-3.

Reflection

1. How do you respond when Christian work is marred by conflict? 2. When is it right to leave?

Chapter 18 - The Questions She Would Not Hide

Central idea

Back in America, she refused to tidy up her experience, and in No Graven Image and other books she exposed the idols of missionary piety.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 62:8; Exodus 20:4-5; Isaiah 55:8-9.

Reflection

1. What questions have you been hiding from God? 2. Is there a God of your own making you need to give up?

Chapter 19 - Addison Leitch

Central idea

A second marriage, to a Presbyterian theologian, brought companionship and happiness, and then the long nursing of a husband dying of cancer.

Scriptures to revisit

Ecclesiastes 4:9-10; Psalm 90:10-12; Romans 12:15.

Reflection

1. How do you receive happiness that may not last? 2. Whom are you called to care for through illness?

Chapter 20 - Lars, and Magnolia

Central idea

A third marriage, a growing family, books on womanhood that drew praise and criticism, and a home life harder than anyone saw.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 68:6; Ephesians 5:21-33; Galatians 3:28.

Reflection

1. How do you weigh teaching on men and women under Scripture with fairness to those who disagree? 2. Is there anyone whose public face hides private burdens you could help to carry?

Chapter 21 - Gateway to Joy

Central idea

For thirteen years a daily radio programme told listeners they were loved with an everlasting love, and that small duties are holy.

Scriptures to revisit

Jeremiah 31:3; Deuteronomy 33:27; Luke 16:10.

Reflection

1. Do you believe you are loved with an everlasting love? 2. Which ordinary duty could you offer to God today?

Chapter 22 - The Next Thing

Central idea

An old poem’s counsel to do the next duty, a conviction that suffering is never wasted, and a willingness to correct her own most famous story.

Scriptures to revisit

Ecclesiastes 9:10; Matthew 6:34; Ephesians 4:25.

Reflection

1. What is the next thing in front of you? 2. Is there a story you have told about God that you need to tell more truthfully?

Chapter 23 - The Long Twilight

Central idea

Dementia silenced the woman who had lived by words, and she was cared for at home until her death on 15 June 2015.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 46:4; Psalm 71:9, 18; 2 Corinthians 4:16-18.

Reflection

1. How do you think about growing old, and about losing your powers? 2. How can your church honour the elderly and those who care for them?

Chapter 24 - The Legacy of Elisabeth Elliot

Central idea

Her books, her family’s publications and honest biographies have kept her witness alive, together with the places where her teaching must be weighed.

Scriptures to revisit

Hebrews 13:7; 1 Thessalonians 5:21; Hebrews 12:1-2.

Reflection

1. Whose faith have you been asked to follow, and how do you test it? 2. What would you want said about the end of your own life?

fields.title: Appendix C: Chronology of the Life and Times of Elisabeth Elliot
fields.body_html:
“My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me.”

— Psalm 31:15, KJV

The dates below are meant as orientation. Where the sources disagree, or where a date is approximate, that is noted.

1926 – Elisabeth Howard is born on 21 December in Brussels, Belgium, the second child of Philip E. Howard Jr. and Katharine Gillingham Howard, missionaries. The family returns to the United States while she is a baby.

1927 – Jim Elliot is born on 8 October in Portland, Oregon.

1930s – The Howards live in Germantown, Philadelphia, and in 1936 move to Moorestown, New Jersey. Philip Howard becomes editor of the Sunday School Times. The family grows to six children: Philip, Elisabeth, David, Virginia, Thomas and James. Summers are spent at Gale Cottage, Franconia, New Hampshire.

1939–1945 – The Second World War.

1941–1944 – Elisabeth attends Hampden DuBose Academy, a Christian boarding school in Florida.

1944–1948 – Wheaton College, Illinois, where she studies classical Greek with a view to Bible translation. She meets Jim Elliot, a friend of her brother Dave.

1948–1952 – A restrained courtship, conducted largely by letter. Elisabeth studies at Prairie Bible Institute, Three Hills, Alberta, and trains in linguistics with the Summer Institute of Linguistics.

1949 – Jim Elliot graduates from Wheaton. On 28 October he writes in his journal that he is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.

1952 – Jim Elliot and Pete Fleming arrive in Ecuador in February. Elisabeth goes to Ecuador independently later in the year and works among the Colorado (Tsáchila) people at San Miguel de los Colorados. The Shandia station is destroyed by a flood.

1952–1953 – During her first year in Ecuador her language helper, Don Macario, is murdered; later a suitcase containing much of her language work is stolen.

1953 – Elisabeth and Jim are engaged in Quito in January. She learns Quichua in the eastern jungle. They marry in a civil ceremony in Quito on 8 October, Jim’s twenty-sixth birthday, and live among the Quichua at Shandia and Puyupungu.

1955 – Valerie Elliot is born on 27 February. From about September or October Nate Saint and his companions make gift drops to a Waorani settlement.

1956 – On 3 January the five missionaries land on “Palm Beach”, a sandbar on the Curaray. Friendly contact follows on 6 January. On 8 January Jim Elliot, Pete Fleming, Ed McCully, Roger Youderian and Nate Saint are speared to death. Life magazine publishes a photo essay. Elisabeth stays at Shandia and continues the Quichua work.

1957 – Through Gates of Splendor is published. Rachel Saint and Dayuma appear on the television programme This Is Your Life (June) and at Billy Graham’s Madison Square Garden crusade (July). In November two Waorani women, Mintaka and Mankamu, come out of the forest and live with Elisabeth.

1958 – Shadow of the Almighty, the life and journals of Jim Elliot, is published. In September Dayuma, Mintaka and Mankamu go back to their people and return about three weeks later with an invitation. In October (on the 8th, by the date usually given) Elisabeth, Valerie and Rachel Saint go with Dayuma and the two women to live among the Waorani, who call Elisabeth Gikari.

1961 – The Savage My Kinsman is published. Late in the year Elisabeth leaves the Waorani and returns to Quichua work.

1963 – Elisabeth and Valerie return to the United States and settle in Franconia, New Hampshire.

1965 – Kimo and Dyuwi baptise Steve and Kathy Saint, Nate Saint’s children, in the Curaray.

1966 – No Graven Image, a novel, is published.

1968 – The Liberty of Obedience and Who Shall Ascend, a life of R. Kenneth Strachan, are published. Margaret Leitch, wife of the theologian Addison H. Leitch, dies.

1969 – On 1 January Elisabeth marries Addison Leitch. They move to Hamilton, Massachusetts, where he teaches theology at the newly formed Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary.

1973 – Addison Leitch dies of cancer on 17 September, aged sixty-four (a few sources give 18 September).

1974–1976 – Elisabeth serves as an adjunct professor at Gordon-Conwell.

1975 – These Strange Ashes, an account of her first year in Ecuador, is published.

1976 – Let Me Be a Woman is published. In the mid-1970s Valerie, engaged at the end of 1974, marries Walter Shepard; they later have eight children.

1977 – In December Elisabeth marries Lars Gren (born 1936), a former salesman trained as a hospital chaplain, who had lodged in her home. They later live in Magnolia, Massachusetts.

1981 – The Mark of a Man is published. She is writer-in-residence at Gordon College.

1982 – Discipline: The Glad Surrender is published. The Elisabeth Elliot Newsletter begins.

1984 – Passion and Purity is published.

1987 – A Chance to Die: The Life and Legacy of Amy Carmichael is published.

1988 – Gateway to Joy begins on Back to the Bible radio. Loneliness is published.

1989–1990 – On Asking God Why (1989) and A Path Through Suffering (1990).

1992 – The Shaping of a Christian Family is published.

1995–1996 – Keep a Quiet Heart (1995) and Quest for Love (1996). A new edition of Through Gates of Splendor (1996) adds an epilogue acknowledging that events among the Waorani had not unfolded simply.

Late 1990s–about 2000 – Her memory begins to fail, and she is diagnosed with dementia; accounts differ over the year.

2001 – Gateway to Joy ends after thirteen years.

2002–2003 – Secure in the Everlasting Arms (2002) and Be Still My Soul (2003).

2003–2004 – The newsletter ends (2003), and she gives up public speaking (2004).

2006 – End of the Spear, a feature film about the events of 1956 and the friendship of Steve Saint and Mincaye, is released.

2015 – Elisabeth Elliot dies at home in Magnolia on 15 June, aged eighty-eight. Her funeral is held on 23 June at Gordon College, Wenham, and a memorial service at Wheaton College on 26 July.

2019 – Valerie Elliot Shepard publishes Devotedly, from her parents’ letters and journals. Kathryn T. Long publishes God in the Rainforest.

2020 – Ellen Vaughn publishes Becoming Elisabeth Elliot, the first volume of the authorised biography.

2023 – Vaughn’s second volume, Being Elisabeth Elliot, and Lucy S. R. Austen’s Elisabeth Elliot: A Life are published.

2025 – Lars Gren dies in Little Rock, Arkansas, on 2 April, aged eighty-eight.

fields.title: Appendix D: Notes on Sources and Method
fields.body_html:
“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”

— 1 Thessalonians 5:21, KJV

About This Work

This book is an independent biography written by Ochorus. It is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by the family or estate of Elisabeth Elliot, or by any publisher, foundation, broadcaster or other organisation that holds rights in her writings and recordings. Her books, letters, newsletters and broadcasts remain in copyright, and they should be obtained from their publishers or borrowed from a library. Readers are warmly encouraged to do so. Nothing in this book can replace the clarity and directness of her own voice.

The book tells her life in its own words. It does not quote Elisabeth Elliot anywhere. Everything it reports of what she thought, felt, wrote or taught is paraphrased, no letter, journal entry, newsletter or broadcast of hers is reproduced, and her books are described rather than retold. The only words quoted, apart from Scripture, are these:

Jim Elliot’s journal, 28 October 1949. His sentence about the man who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose, quoted once, in the chapter “Palm Beach”.

“Doe the Nexte Thynge”. The anonymous nineteenth-century poem she often cited, which is in the public domain: its refrain, in the chapters “The Widow at Shandia” and “The Next Thing”, and its opening line, in “The Next Thing”.

Amy Carmichael. Two brief phrases from her public-domain writing: the refrain of If, in the chapter “Hampden DuBose”, and a phrase from the poem that gave These Strange Ashes its title, in “Macario, and a Stolen Suitcase”.

Scripture. All Scripture is quoted from the King James Version.

Primary Sources

Elisabeth Elliot’s own books are the first source for her life, and the most important are named in the chapters where they belong. Through Gates of Splendor (1957; new edition with an epilogue, 1996) tells the story of the five missionaries. Shadow of the Almighty (1958) is her life of Jim Elliot, built around his journals and letters, and she later edited The Journals of Jim Elliot (1978). The Savage My Kinsman (1961) records, chiefly in photographs, her time among the Waorani. These Strange Ashes (1975) describes her first year in Ecuador among the Colorados. Passion and Purity (1984) tells the story of her courtship with Jim, and The Shaping of a Christian Family (1992) describes the home in which she grew up. Her novel No Graven Image (1966) is not autobiography, but it draws closely on her own experience.

Valerie Elliot Shepard’s Devotedly: The Personal Letters and Love Story of Jim and Elisabeth Elliot (2019) publishes a large selection of her parents’ letters and journals from the years of their courtship and marriage.

Biographies and Studies

This book is particularly indebted to the following, which readers who want to go further will find rewarding:

Ellen Vaughn, Becoming Elisabeth Elliot (2020) and Being Elisabeth Elliot (2023). The authorised biography, written with access to her surviving journals and letters. The second volume is the fullest published account of her later years, including her marriages to Addison Leitch and Lars Gren.

Lucy S. R. Austen, Elisabeth Elliot: A Life (2023). An independent full-length biography based on long study of the sources.

Kathryn T. Long, God in the Rainforest: A Tale of Martyrdom and Redemption in Amazonian Ecuador (2019). A historian’s account of the missionary encounter with the Waorani from the 1950s onward, giving full weight to the Waorani themselves and to the tensions among the missionaries.

Russell T. Hitt, Jungle Pilot (1959). The life of Nate Saint, drawing on his letters and diaries.

Olive Fleming Liefeld, Unfolding Destinies. The story of Pete Fleming and of the years after 1956, told by his widow.

Corrections and Disputed Points

The Waorani. The people who killed the five missionaries were widely called “Auca” in the 1950s, a Quichua word meaning roughly “savage”, which they regarded as an insult. This book uses their own name, Waorani, except where the older label is part of a historical title such as Operation Auca.

The 1956 story. The early accounts, including Elisabeth Elliot’s own, were written within months of the deaths and inevitably simplified a complicated history. Her 1996 epilogue, and the work of Long and others, have qualified them. Where later research differs from the first telling, this book follows the later research.

Addison Leitch. Most sources give 17 September 1973 as the date of his death, a few the 18th, and they differ on exactly when and where he and Elisabeth first met. The account given here keeps to what the sources agree on.

Lars Gren. Our knowledge of Elisabeth Elliot’s third marriage rests largely on Ellen Vaughn’s Being Elisabeth Elliot, which draws on the testimony of family and friends gathered after her death, because, as Vaughn reports, most of her journals from those years were destroyed. Lars Gren, who died in 2025, did not give his own account, and his view of the marriage is largely missing from the record. This book reports only what that published biography describes, attributes it to Vaughn, and records equally his many years of care for Elisabeth in her illness, without attempting to judge between them.

Her teaching on women. Her views on men, women, marriage and submission were embraced by many readers and criticised by others, including evangelicals who hold that Scripture teaches the equality of men and women in the home and the church. This book describes the debate but does not try to settle it; the teaching itself is weighed in the companion volume, The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot.

Quotations attributed to her. Many sayings circulate under her name, and not all of them are hers. Readers who wish to quote her should check the words against her own books.

The Library She Loved

Several of the books that shaped Elisabeth and Jim Elliot are in the public domain and in the Ochorus library. Amy Carmichael’s Things as They Are and If come from the missionary whose life Elisabeth later wrote. The Life and Diary of David Brainerd was a model for Jim Elliot’s own devotion and for his journal. Hudson Taylor’s A Retrospect tells the story of a missionary who learned, as she did, to trust God for the next step. Thomas à Kempis’s The Imitation of Christ and Brother Lawrence’s The Practice of the Presence of God belong to the tradition of practical, daily devotion she commended. Jim Elliot also has an author page on Ochorus. All of these can be read freely there, alongside the companion volume The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot.

Scripture

All Scripture quotations are from the Authorised (King James) Version, which is in the public domain.
